docs.text: Rendered as separate note messages or tooltips.

docs.title: Multiple Annotations
docs.text:
A flow can have multiple annotations:

{
  "annotations": [
    {"type": "security", "text": "Requires TLS 1.3"},
    {"type": "security", "text": "Validate client certificate"},
    {"type": "performance", "text": "Response cached for 5 minutes"}
  ]
}

docs.title: vs Notes
docs.text:
Feature note annotations Structure Plain string Typed objects Multiple No Yes Metadata No Type + details Tooling Display only Processable

Use note for simple display text. Use annotations for structured metadata that tools can process.

docs.title: Helper Methods (Go)
docs.text:
// Check if flow has annotations
if flow.HasAnnotations() {
    for _, ann := range flow.Annotations {
        fmt.Printf("[%s] %s\n", ann.Type, ann.Text)
    }
}

// Validate annotation type
if pidl.IsValidAnnotationType("security") {
    // valid
}

docs.title: Embedding the Viewer
docs.text:
The walkthrough viewer comes in two forms that read the same walkthrough format:

Form Use it for pidl generate -f viewer one self-contained HTML file, for offline use, email or opening from disk (Walkthrough Viewer) @grokify/pidl-viewer a script any page loads from a CDN, to show one or more walkthroughs inside docs, blogs or apps

docs.title: Publish a Walkthrough
docs.text:
Generate the walkthrough and host it next to your pages, or anywhere that serves it over HTTPS:

pidl generate -f walkthrough-json -o api.walkthrough.json oauth2_api_access

Generate it in CI from the PIDL source rather than committing it, so it never falls behind the protocol.

docs.title: One Script Tag
docs.text:
<div id="walkthrough"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"
        data-pidl-target="#walkthrough"
        data-pidl-src="api.walkthrough.json"></script>

The script mounts the viewer on the element named by data-pidl-target once the page has loaded. It reads the walkthrough from the first of these that is present:

Attribute Walkthrough data-pidl-data="<id>" the JSON inside <script type="application/json" id="<id>"> on the page data-pidl-src="<url>" the URL, relative to the page (neither) the page's ?src= query parameter

docs.title: A Complete Page
docs.text:
A page that shows one walkthrough needs nothing else, much as a Swagger UI page needs only its script and the URL of an OpenAPI document:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>API Access Walkthrough</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; }
    #walkthrough { height: 100vh; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <div id="walkthrough"></div>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"
          data-pidl-target="#walkthrough"
          data-pidl-src="api.walkthrough.json"></script>
</body>
</html>

Put api.walkthrough.json next to the page, or give data-pidl-src a full URL.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Every version on npm is on jsDelivr at https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@<version>/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js, and on unpkg at the same path under https://unpkg.com/.

  • Name an exact version, such as @0.9.0. A file at an exact version never changes, so a new release cannot change your pages. A range such as @0.9 follows new releases, but CDNs cache it for days, so pages can show different versions for a while.
  • Check the file with Subresource Integrity. Add the file's hash and crossorigin, and the browser refuses the script if the CDN ever serves anything else:
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"
        integrity="sha384-<hash>"
        crossorigin="anonymous"
        data-pidl-target="#walkthrough"
        data-pidl-src="api.walkthrough.json"></script>

jsDelivr shows the hash on the package's page; to compute it yourself:

curl -s https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js \
  | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A

docs.title: Inline Data
docs.text:
<div id="walkthrough"></div>
<script type="application/json" id="api-data">
  { "format": "pidl-walkthrough/v1", "id": "oauth2-api-access", ... }
</script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"
        data-pidl-target="#walkthrough"
        data-pidl-data="api-data"></script>

docs.title: One Page for Any Walkthrough
docs.text:
A page with a script tag that names no walkthrough shows the one in its ?src= parameter, so one page can show any walkthrough:

https://example.com/viewer.html?src=https://example.org/api.walkthrough.json

?src= loads only https: URLs, or URLs on the page's own origin. The top bar names the host a walkthrough came from when it is not the page's own, so readers can tell whose content they are reading.

docs.title: From JavaScript
docs.text:
PidlViewer.mount renders a walkthrough into an element and returns a promise for the viewer:

<div id="a"></div>
<div id="b"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"></script>
<script>
  PidlViewer.mount(document.getElementById("a"), { src: "api.walkthrough.json" });
  PidlViewer.mount(document.getElementById("b"), { data: myWalkthrough });
</script>

As an ES module, with types, from npm or a CDN:

import { mount } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.mjs";

const viewer = await mount(document.querySelector("#walkthrough"), { src: "api.walkthrough.json" });
// later: viewer.unmount();
Option Meaning data a walkthrough, parsed or as JSON text src the URL of a walkthrough, relative to the page base the URL relative paths inside the walkthrough resolve against (default: src) hash keep the scenario and step in the page's URL hash (default: false)

mount resolves once the walkthrough is shown, and rejects, after showing the error in the element, when it cannot load. The package also exports the walkthrough types and WALKTHROUGH_FORMAT, and ships the schema as @grokify/pidl-viewer/walkthrough.schema.json.

docs.title: On the Page
docs.text:
• Size. The viewer fills its element, which is 720px tall unless your page sets a height, for example #walkthrough { height: 80vh; }. It is laid out for widths of about 1000px and up.
  • Styles. The viewer renders inside a shadow root, so your page's styles do not change it and its styles do not leak into your page.
  • Keys. An embedded viewer takes the step keys (→, ←, Home, End, P) only while it has focus; click it first. The standalone page takes them anywhere.
  • Position. An auto-mounted viewer that is the only one on its page keeps the scenario and step in the URL hash, so links open at a step. Otherwise each viewer keeps its position to itself, unless you pass hash: true.
  • Theme and presenting. Theme and Present work as on the standalone page; Present fills the browser window.

docs.title: Hosting the Walkthrough
docs.text:
• CORS. A walkthrough on another origin must be served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. GitHub Pages and raw.githubusercontent.com send it; for your own server, allow at least the origins of the pages that embed it.
  • Credentials. The viewer fetches walkthroughs without cookies or other credentials, so a walkthrough must be readable without signing in.
  • Content. The viewer treats a walkthrough as data: it shows its text as text, never as HTML, and opens only http: and https: links from it.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text: Entities represent participants in the protocol: systems, services, actors, or trust domains.

docs.title: Extending PIDL
docs.text: This guide explains how to extend PIDL with custom renderers, validation rules, and exporters.

docs.title: Custom Renderers
docs.text: PIDL uses a Renderer interface that you can implement to create custom diagram output formats.

docs.title: The Renderer Interface
docs.text:
package render

import (
    "io"
    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
)

type Renderer interface {
    // Render writes the diagram to the writer.
    Render(w io.Writer, p *pidl.Protocol) error

    // RenderString returns the diagram as a string.
    RenderString(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error)

    // Format returns the output format name.
    Format() Format
}

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Renderer
docs.text:
Here's a complete example of a custom Markdown renderer:

package render

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "strings"

    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
)

// MyMarkdownRenderer generates a custom Markdown format.
type MyMarkdownRenderer struct {
    // Title includes the protocol name as header.
    Title bool
    // ShowDescriptions includes flow descriptions.
    ShowDescriptions bool
}

// NewMyMarkdown creates a new renderer with defaults.
func NewMyMarkdown() *MyMarkdownRenderer {
    return &MyMarkdownRenderer{
        Title:            true,
        ShowDescriptions: true,
    }
}

// Format returns the format identifier.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) Format() Format {
    return Format("my-markdown")
}

// Render writes the Markdown to the writer.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) Render(w io.Writer, p *pidl.Protocol) error {
    s, err := r.RenderString(p)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = w.Write([]byte(s))
    return err
}

// RenderString returns the Markdown as a string.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) RenderString(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    var sb strings.Builder

    // Write title
    if r.Title {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("# %s\n\n", p.ProtocolMeta.Name))
    }

    // Write entities
    sb.WriteString("## Entities\n\n")
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("- **%s** (%s)\n", e.Name, e.Type))
    }
    sb.WriteString("\n")

    // Write flows
    sb.WriteString("## Flows\n\n")
    for i, f := range p.Flows {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("%d. %s → %s: %s\n",
            i+1, f.From, f.To, f.Label))
        if r.ShowDescriptions && f.Description != "" {
            sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("   - %s\n", f.Description))
        }
    }

    return sb.String(), nil
}

docs.title: Registering a Custom Renderer
docs.text:
To integrate your renderer with the render.New() factory:

// In your application code
func init() {
    // Register with the format parser
    render.RegisterFormat("my-markdown", func() render.Renderer {
        return NewMyMarkdown()
    })
}

Or use it directly:

renderer := NewMyMarkdown()
output, err := renderer.RenderString(protocol)

docs.title: Best Practices for Renderers
docs.text:
1. Support configuration options - Use struct fields for customization
  2. Handle both io.Writer and string output - Implement both methods
  3. Check protocol kind - Process specs may need different handling
  4. Handle empty protocols gracefully - Don't panic on missing data
  5. Consider step types - For process specs, use StepType for visual differentiation

docs.title: Custom Validation Rules
docs.text: PIDL's security analysis system uses rules that can be extended.

docs.title: The SecurityRule Structure
docs.text:
type SecurityRule struct {
    // ID is a unique identifier (e.g., "SEC001")
    ID string

    // Name is a human-readable name
    Name string

    // Description explains what the rule checks
    Description string

    // Category groups related rules
    Category string

    // Severity indicates the risk level
    Severity Severity

    // Check is the function that evaluates the rule
    Check func(p *pidl.Protocol, opts *AnalysisOptions) []Risk
}

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Rule
docs.text:
package analyze

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

// MyCustomRule checks for a specific security pattern.
var MyCustomRule = SecurityRule{
    ID:          "CUSTOM001",
    Name:        "Unencrypted Sensitive Data",
    Description: "Sensitive data should use encryption",
    Category:    CategoryDataProtection,
    Severity:    SeverityHigh,
    Check: func(p *pidl.Protocol, opts *AnalysisOptions) []Risk {
        var risks []Risk

        for _, flow := range p.Flows {
            // Check if flow has sensitive data
            if flow.Annotation != nil && flow.Annotation.DataClassification == "confidential" {
                // Check if encryption is required
                if !hasSecurityRequirement(flow, "encryption") {
                    risks = append(risks, Risk{
                        RuleID:      "CUSTOM001",
                        Severity:    SeverityHigh,
                        Category:    CategoryDataProtection,
                        Location:    fmt.Sprintf("flow %s→%s", flow.From, flow.To),
                        Message:     "Confidential data transmitted without encryption",
                        Remediation: "Add security requirement: encryption",
                    })
                }
            }
        }

        return risks
    },
}

func hasSecurityRequirement(flow pidl.Flow, req string) bool {
    if flow.Security == nil {
        return false
    }
    for _, r := range flow.Security.Requires {
        if r == req {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

docs.title: Registering Custom Rules
docs.text:
// Add your rule to the analyzer
func init() {
    analyze.RegisterRule(MyCustomRule)
}

// Or create a custom analyzer
analyzer := analyze.NewAnalyzer()
analyzer.AddRule(MyCustomRule)

results := analyzer.Analyze(protocol)

docs.title: Rule Categories
docs.text: Category Description CategoryAuthentication Identity verification issues CategoryAuthorization Access control issues CategoryTokenSecurity Token handling issues CategoryDataProtection Data security issues CategoryNetworkSecurity Network boundary issues CategoryProcessSecurity Process spec issues

docs.title: Severity Levels
docs.text: Severity When to Use SeverityCritical Immediate security threat SeverityHigh Significant security risk SeverityMedium Moderate security concern SeverityLow Minor issue or best practice SeverityInfo Informational finding

docs.title: Custom Exporters
docs.text: Workflow exporters convert PIDL process specs to executable formats.

docs.title: The Exporter Pattern
docs.text:
package export

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

type MyExporter struct {
    // Configuration options
    OutputFormat string
}

func NewMyExporter() *MyExporter {
    return &MyExporter{
        OutputFormat: "default",
    }
}

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Validate it's a process spec
    if p.ProtocolMeta.Kind != pidl.ProtocolKindProcess {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("only process specs supported")
    }

    // Build your output format
    var sb strings.Builder

    for _, entity := range p.Entities {
        if entity.StepType == "" {
            continue
        }

        // Generate code for this step
        sb.WriteString(e.generateStep(entity))
    }

    return sb.String(), nil
}

func (e *MyExporter) generateStep(entity pidl.Entity) string {
    // Step-type-specific code generation
    switch entity.StepType {
    case pidl.StepTypeDeterministic:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Deterministic: %s\n", entity.Name)
    case pidl.StepTypeLLM:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// LLM: %s\n", entity.Name)
    case pidl.StepTypeHuman:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Human: %s\n", entity.Name)
    default:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Step: %s\n", entity.Name)
    }
}

docs.title: Using Parallel Block Detection
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Detect parallel execution blocks
    blocks := pidl.DetectParallelBlocks(p)

    for _, block := range blocks {
        fmt.Printf("Parallel block: %s\n", block.ID)
        fmt.Printf("  Join condition: %s\n", block.JoinCondition)

        for _, branch := range block.Branches {
            fmt.Printf("  Branch: %s\n", branch.EntityID)
        }
    }

    // Use execution graph for ordering
    graph := pidl.AnalyzeExecutionGraph(p)
    for _, stage := range graph.Stages {
        fmt.Printf("Stage %s: %v\n", stage.ID, stage.Steps)
    }

    return "", nil
}

docs.title: Using Cost Information
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Analyze costs
    analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessCosts(p)

    fmt.Printf("Total estimated cost: $%.4f\n",
        analysis.TotalEstimate.ExpectedCost)

    for stepType, cost := range analysis.CostByType {
        fmt.Printf("  %s: $%.4f\n", stepType, cost)
    }

    return "", nil
}

docs.title: Schema Validation Extension
docs.text: You can extend schema validation with custom validators.

docs.title: Custom Port Validator
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

type CustomValidator struct {
    *pidl.PortSchemaValidator
    customRules []func(port pidl.DataPort, data interface{}) error
}

func NewCustomValidator() *CustomValidator {
    return &CustomValidator{
        PortSchemaValidator: pidl.NewPortSchemaValidator(),
    }
}

func (v *CustomValidator) AddRule(rule func(pidl.DataPort, interface{}) error) {
    v.customRules = append(v.customRules, rule)
}

func (v *CustomValidator) ValidatePortData(port pidl.DataPort, data interface{}) (*pidl.SchemaValidationResult, error) {
    // Run base validation
    result, err := v.PortSchemaValidator.ValidatePortData(port, data)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // Run custom rules
    for _, rule := range v.customRules {
        if err := rule(port, data); err != nil {
            result.Valid = false
            result.Errors = append(result.Errors, pidl.SchemaValidationError{
                Path:    port.Name,
                Message: err.Error(),
            })
        }
    }

    return result, nil
}

docs.title: Testing Renderers
docs.text:
func TestMyRenderer(t *testing.T) {
    p := &pidl.Protocol{
        ProtocolMeta: pidl.ProtocolMeta{
            ID:   "test",
            Name: "Test Protocol",
        },
        Entities: []pidl.Entity{
            {ID: "a", Name: "Service A"},
            {ID: "b", Name: "Service B"},
        },
        Flows: []pidl.Flow{
            {From: "a", To: "b", Label: "Request"},
        },
    }

    r := NewMyMarkdown()
    output, err := r.RenderString(p)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("Render failed: %v", err)
    }

    if !strings.Contains(output, "# Test Protocol") {
        t.Error("expected title in output")
    }
}

func TestMyCustomRule(t *testing.T) {
    p := &pidl.Protocol{
        // ... protocol with security issue
    }

docs.title: Flows
docs.text: Flows are the core semantic unit: directed interactions between entities.

docs.title: Basic Flow
docs.text:
{
  "flows": [
    {
      "from": "client",
      "to": "server",
      "action": "request",
      "label": "GET /resource",
      "mode": "request"
    },
    {
      "from": "server",
      "to": "client",
      "action": "response",
      "label": "200 OK",
      "mode": "response"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Flow Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description from string Yes Source entity ID to string Yes Target entity ID action string Yes Action identifier label string No Display label (defaults to action) mode enum No Interaction mode (defaults to request) phase string No Phase ID this flow belongs to description string No Detailed description sequence integer No Deprecated. Display-only step number; never affects order condition string No Conditional execution clause note string No Visible note on diagram annotations array No Typed annotations alternatives array No Alternative flow paths verification object No Evidentiary provenance (see Verification)

docs.title: Flow Modes
docs.text: Mode Description Arrow Style request Synchronous request Solid -> response Synchronous response Dashed --> redirect HTTP redirect Solid with annotation callback Callback/webhook Solid with annotation interactive Human interaction Solid event Asynchronous event Dashed tool_call Tool invocation (MCP) Solid with annotation tool_result Tool result (MCP) Dashed with annotation

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Flows run in array order. To change the order, move the flow in the array.

The sequence field is deprecated. It is a display-only step number and does not reorder flows. See Ordering in the specification for the rules that apply to entities, phases and scenarios.

docs.title: Conditional Flows
docs.text:
Use condition to specify when a flow executes:

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "refresh_token",
  "condition": "token_expired"
}

Renders as opt block in sequence diagrams.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Add visible notes to flows:

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "authenticate",
  "note": "Requires TLS 1.3"
}

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
For incident attack-flows, a flow can record its evidentiary provenance — how well-substantiated the step is and where it is sourced from. This lets a published attack chain distinguish a step observed in a primary source from one that is inferred.

{
  "from": "agent-collective",
  "to": "hugging-face",
  "action": "exploit_worker",
  "verification": {
    "tier": "corroborated",
    "source": "METR",
    "citation": "https://metr.org/..."
  }
}
Field Type Required Description tier enum Yes reported | corroborated | reproduced | partially_reproduced source string No Originating source (e.g. "OpenAI technical report", "METR") citation string No URL or reference locating the source

The tier vocabulary matches the aisecurity-incidents deepdive.json. Sequence renderers emit a compact provenance badge (e.g. 🔎 corroborated — METR), toggled by the renderer's ShowVerification option, and the security analyzer flags flows below the corroborated tier.

See also:

  • Annotations for typed metadata
  • Alternatives for branching paths

docs.title: PIDL Format
docs.text:
A PIDL document is a JSON file with four sections:

{
  "protocol": { ... },
  "entities": [ ... ],
  "phases": [ ... ],
  "flows": [ ... ]
}
Section Required Description protocol Yes Metadata about the protocol entities Yes Participants in the protocol (min 2) phases No Logical grouping of flows flows Yes Interactions between entities (min 1)

docs.title: Protocol Metadata
docs.text:
{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "oauth2-authorization-code",
    "name": "OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow",
    "version": "1.0",
    "description": "OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Grant",
    "category": "auth",
    "references": [
      {
        "name": "RFC 6749",
        "url": "https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749"
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Protocol Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier (lowercase, alphanumeric, hyphens) name string Yes Human-readable name version string No Version of this protocol description description string No Brief description category enum No One of: auth, agent, messaging, provisioning, other references array No Links to specifications

docs.title: File Extension
docs.text: PIDL files use the .pidl.json extension by convention.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Use the CLI to validate files:

pidl validate protocol.json

Or programmatically:

p, _ := pidl.ParseFile("protocol.json")
if errs := p.Validate(); errs.HasErrors() {
    fmt.Println(errs)
}

docs.title: Narration
docs.text:
Narration is text written to be spoken: the script for audio, autoplay and narrated video of a walkthrough. It is separate from description because on-screen prose reads badly aloud. A description can say "the server compares the SHA-256 of code_verifier with code_challenge"; a narrator should say "the server checks the secret against the challenge".

PIDL keeps narration in the document, beside the steps it describes, and passes it into the walkthrough, where audio and video tools read it. The walkthrough viewer does not play narration yet.

docs.title: Narration by Language
docs.text:
Every narration value is an object keyed by BCP 47 language tag. Scenarios and flows carry it:

{
  "protocol": {"id": "oauth2-api-access", "name": "OAuth 2.0 API Access", "language": "en-US"},
  "scenarios": [{
    "id": "authorization-code",
    "name": "Authorization code with PKCE",
    "narration": {
      "en-US": "A user lets an application read their reports.",
      "fr-FR": "Un utilisateur autorise une application à lire ses rapports."
    },
    "flows": [{
      "id": "token-request",
      "from": "client", "to": "as", "action": "token_request",
      "narration": {"en-US": "The application trades the code for a token."}
    }]
  }]
}

protocol.language is the language the document is written in, en-US unless set. Every narration object must include it, and it is the fallback for any language a narration lacks, so a partly translated document still narrates every step.

Include steps carry no narration; the steps of their fragment do.

docs.title: Briefings
docs.text:
A briefing introduces a scenario before its first step: why it matters, and what to watch for. Video tools show it as an opening slide.

"briefing": {
  "why": "The client never sees the user's credentials, and a stolen code is useless without the PKCE verifier.",
  "points": ["The browser carries the code, not the token", "PKCE binds the code to the client that asked for it"],
  "narration": {"en-US": "Why the authorization code grant with PKCE is the default."}
}

docs.title: Representations
docs.text:
A reader can view a step as HTTP, as a curl command or as a code sample. A step's representations override its narration for one of those views, so the Go tab can talk about the code rather than the wire format:

{
  "id": "token-request",
  "from": "client", "to": "as", "action": "token_request",
  "narration": {"en-US": "The application trades the code for a token."},
  "representations": {
    "curl": {"narration": {"en-US": "This curl command posts the form the token endpoint expects."}},
    "go": {"narration": {"en-US": "Exchange sends the code and the verifier in one call."}}
  }
}

The keys are http, curl, or a language of one of the step's samples. For a reader's language and representation, the spoken text is the first of these that exists:

  1. The representation's narration in the reader's language
  2. The representation's narration in the source language
  3. The step's narration in the reader's language
  4. The step's narration in the source language
  5. The step's description

docs.title: Pronunciations
docs.text:
Pronunciations map a term to how it is spoken, per language:

"pronunciations": {
  "PKCE": {"en-US": "pixy"},
  "OAuth": {"en-US": "oh auth"}
}

They use the shape videoascode reads, so text-to-speech tools can use them unchanged. Pronunciations from documents named by extends and imports are merged in.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: pidl validate checks that narration keys are BCP 47 tags with non-empty text, that every narration object includes the source language, that representation keys are http, curl or a sample language on that step, and that include steps carry no narration.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Scenarios
  • Code Samples and cURL
  • Specification: Narration

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phases provide logical grouping of flows for readability and diagram organization.

docs.title: Basic Phases
docs.text:
{
  "phases": [
    {
      "id": "authorization",
      "name": "Authorization",
      "description": "User authentication and consent"
    },
    {
      "id": "token_exchange",
      "name": "Token Exchange",
      "description": "Exchange code for tokens"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Phase Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier name string Yes Human-readable name description string No Phase description parent string No Parent phase ID for nesting

docs.title: Nested Phases
docs.text:
Phases support hierarchical nesting via the parent field:

{
  "phases": [
    {"id": "auth", "name": "Authentication"},
    {"id": "login", "name": "Login", "parent": "auth"},
    {"id": "mfa", "name": "Multi-Factor Auth", "parent": "auth"},
    {"id": "token", "name": "Token Exchange"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Hierarchy Rules
docs.text:
• A phase with no parent is a root phase
  • A phase with a parent must reference a valid phase ID
  • Circular references are not allowed
  • A phase cannot be its own parent

docs.title: Assigning Flows to Phases
docs.text:
Reference the phase ID in flows:

{
  "flows": [
    {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "login", "phase": "login"},
    {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "mfa_challenge", "phase": "mfa"},
    {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "token_request", "phase": "token"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Diagram Rendering
docs.text: Format Rendering PlantUML Colored box containers Mermaid Colored rect blocks D2 Nested groups DOT Subgraphs (if enabled)

docs.title: Helper Methods (Go)
docs.text:
// Get root phases (no parent)
roots := protocol.RootPhases()

// Get children of a phase
children := protocol.ChildPhases("auth")

// Get nesting depth (0 for root)
depth := protocol.PhaseDepth("mfa")  // returns 1 if parent is "auth"

docs.title: Postman Collections
docs.text:
pidl generate -f postman turns a PIDL file into a Postman collection you can run: a folder for each scenario, a request for each step the client role sends, values passed from each response to the next request, and checks on every response. The collection is generated from the same examples the walkthrough viewer shows, so the two agree step for step.

# Signed requests sent through a signing proxy
pidl generate -f postman --signer proxy -o api.postman_collection.json oauth2_api_access

# Requests sent directly, with saved example responses for a Postman mock server
pidl generate -f postman --mock -o api-mock.postman_collection.json oauth2_api_access

docs.title: What Is Generated
docs.text: Part From Folders Groups, then scenarios, in output order; fragments expanded in place Requests Steps whose sender is the client role (--client, default: the first agent or client entity) and that have an example request URLs Each role's base URL becomes a variable such as {{ps_url}} Chained values A value an earlier response delivers (a body member, a Location or another header, or a string parameter of a header, such as the scope of a WWW-Authenticate challenge or a parameter of a structured field) and a later request reuses is saved to a collection variable and referenced as {{name}} Checks Status code; headers named in the example; body members; and the claim names of tokens the body carries Deferred responses A request answered 202 with Location accepts either the 202 (then the next request polls {{location}} until it completes) or the final response (then the poll is skipped) Folder notes The scenario's description and narration, and the steps between other roles that the collection does not send

docs.title: Signing Proxies
docs.text:
Postman cannot create HTTP message signatures (RFC 9421). With --signer proxy, each request whose example is signed goes to {{signer_url}}/<target URL>, and a signing proxy signs it and forwards it. Requests without signatures are sent directly.

Header Sent to the proxy Signature, Signature-Input, Content-Digest Left out; the proxy creates them Signature-Key How to sign: the example's label and scheme, such as sig=hwk. For the jwt scheme it also carries the token to present when an earlier response delivered it, sig=jwt;jwt="{{user_token}}"; without one, the proxy presents its own Everything else As in the example, with chained values

The proxy decides what each token means for its protocol. An implementation of a signed protocol can provide one for testing: the AAuth sandbox in aauth-go is a signing proxy for AAuth.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
An environment says where a target's roles run. Write targets in a JSON file:

{
  "local": {
    "signer": "http://127.0.0.1:8099",
    "roles": {
      "as": "https://as.local.test",
      "api": "https://api.local.test"
    },
    "scenarios": {
      "async-export": {"api": "https://exports.local.test"}
    }
  },
  "mock": {
    "roles": {"as": "{{mock_url}}", "api": "{{mock_url}}"},
    "variables": {"mock_url": "https://<your-mock-id>.mock.pstmn.io"}
  }
}

pidl generate -f postman-environment --targets targets.json --target local -o local.postman_environment.json oauth2_api_access

scenarios points a role at another server for one scenario's folder only: here, the asynchronous export goes to a separate export service. Without --targets, the environment uses the base URLs of the examples.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Import the collection and an environment into Postman and run a folder, or use Newman:

npx newman run api.postman_collection.json -e local.postman_environment.json --folder "Asynchronous export"

Collections are generated output: edit the PIDL file and regenerate rather than editing the collection.

docs.title: Process Specifications
docs.text: PIDL supports two profiles: protocol (default) and process. This guide explains when to use each and how to model process workflows.

docs.title: Protocol vs Process
docs.text: Aspect Protocol Process Focus System interactions Data transformations Entities Services, actors, systems Processing steps Flows Request/response patterns Data flow between steps Primary concern "Who talks to whom" "How data transforms" Output Sequence diagrams Pipeline diagrams

docs.title: When to Use Protocol
docs.text:
Use the protocol profile when modeling:

  • Authentication/authorization flows (OAuth, OIDC, SAML)
  • API choreography between services
  • Agent protocols (MCP, A2A)
  • Multi-party interactions with clear request/response patterns
  • Trust relationships between systems

Example: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, MCP tool invocation.

docs.title: When to Use Process
docs.text:
Use the process profile when modeling:

  • Data pipelines (ETL, data processing)
  • AI/ML workflows with LLM steps
  • Document processing workflows
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Approval workflows with human review

Example: Document extraction → LLM transformation → human review → database load.

docs.title: Defining a Process Spec
docs.text:
Set kind: "process" in the protocol metadata:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "document-pipeline",
    "name": "Document Processing Pipeline",
    "kind": "process"
  }
}

docs.title: Step Types
docs.text:
Each entity in a process spec should have a step_type:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "extract",
      "name": "Extract Data",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "deterministic"
    },
    {
      "id": "summarize",
      "name": "LLM Summarization",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "llm"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Step Type Reference
docs.text: Step Type When to Use Rendering deterministic Predictable transformations, parsing, validation ⚙️ Blue rectangle llm AI/ML processing, text generation, embeddings 🧠 Purple hexagon human Manual review, approval, data entry 👤 Green circle external API calls, third-party services ☁️ Orange cloud tool Function calls, utility operations 🔧 Gray diamond

docs.title: Data Ports
docs.text:
Define explicit inputs and outputs for each step:

{
  "id": "transform",
  "name": "Transform Step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "raw_document",
      "kind": "file",
      "required": true,
      "description": "PDF or text document to process"
    }
  ],
  "outputs": [
    {
      "name": "summary",
      "kind": "object",
      "description": "Structured summary of the document"
    },
    {
      "name": "embeddings",
      "kind": "object",
      "sensitive": false,
      "description": "Vector embeddings for search"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Port Kinds
docs.text: Kind Icon Use For file 📄 Documents, images, binary data object 📦 JSON objects, structs, in-memory data api 🌐 API request/response payloads database 🗄️ Database records, query results queue 📬 Message queue items stream 🌊 Streaming data, real-time feeds

docs.title: Processing Configuration
docs.text:
Configure execution characteristics:

{
  "id": "llm_step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "processing": {
    "engine": "claude-3-opus",
    "deterministic": false,
    "timeout": "PT60S",
    "cache_key": "document_hash"
  }
}

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
Document failure modes and retry strategies:

{
  "id": "api_call",
  "step_type": "external",
  "failure_modes": [
    {
      "id": "timeout",
      "name": "Request Timeout",
      "severity": "medium",
      "recovery": "Retry with exponential backoff"
    }
  ],
  "retry_strategy": {
    "max_attempts": 3,
    "initial_delay": "PT1S",
    "backoff_multiplier": 2.0
  }
}

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Process specs trigger additional security analysis rules:

Rule Severity Issue SEC011 Medium LLM step without downstream validation SEC012 High Sensitive data flows to LLM step SEC013 Medium Non-deterministic step in critical path SEC014 Low External step without failure modes SEC015 Medium Human step without timeout

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate LLM outputs - Add a validation step after LLM processing
  2. Mark sensitive data - Use sensitive: true on ports containing PII
  3. Define failure modes - Document how external steps can fail
  4. Set timeouts - Human steps should have timeouts to prevent blocking
  5. Use deterministic steps - For critical path operations that must be reproducible

docs.title: Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
pidl generate -f svg process.json

Steps are styled by type with icons and colors.

docs.title: Infographic
docs.text:
# LinkedIn-friendly infographic
pidl generate -f infographic --size=linkedin-square --title="My Pipeline" process.json

# Datasheet tile
pidl generate -f infographic --size=datasheet-tile --theme=minimal process.json

Infographics render with:

  • Custom shapes per step type (hexagon for LLM, circle for human, etc.)
  • Animated dots showing data flow
  • Step type icons and colors
  • Compact layout for social media

docs.title: D2 Architecture
docs.text:
pidl generate -f d2-arch --show-ports process.json

Data ports are rendered as connected nodes grouped by kind.

docs.title: Example: Document Review Pipeline
docs.text:
{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "doc-review",
    "name": "Document Review Pipeline",
    "kind": "process"
  },
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "ingest",
      "name": "Document Ingestion",
      "step_type": "deterministic",
      "outputs": [{"name": "document", "kind": "file"}]
    },
    {
      "id": "extract",
      "name": "Content Extraction",
      "step_type": "deterministic",
      "inputs": [{"name": "document", "kind": "file", "required": true}],
      "outputs": [{"name": "content", "kind": "object"}]
    },
    {
      "id": "analyze",
      "name": "LLM Analysis",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "inputs": [{"name": "content", "kind": "object", "required": true}],
      "outputs": [{"name": "analysis", "kind": "object"}],
      "processing": {"engine": "claude-3-opus", "timeout": "PT60S"}
    },
    {
      "id": "review",
      "name": "Human Review",
      "step_type": "human",
      "inputs": [{"name": "analysis", "kind": "object", "required": true}],
      "outputs": [{"name": "approved", "kind": "object"}]
    },
    {
      "id": "store",
      "name": "Store Results",
      "step_type": "external",
      "inputs": [{"name": "approved", "kind": "object", "required": true}],
      "failure_modes": [{"id": "db_error", "severity": "high"}],
      "retry_strategy": {"max_attempts": 3}
    }
  ],
  "flows": [
    {"from": "ingest", "to": "extract", "action": "parse"},
    {"from": "extract", "to": "analyze", "action": "analyze"},
    {"from": "analyze", "to": "review", "action": "review"},
    {"from": "review", "to": "store", "action": "save"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Go Library Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

// Check if protocol is a process spec
if p.IsProcessSpec() {
    // Get process steps
    steps := p.ProcessSteps()

    // Filter by step type
    llmSteps := p.LLMSteps()
    humanSteps := p.HumanSteps()

    // Check individual entities
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        if e.IsLLMStep() {
            // Handle LLM step
        }

        // Get required inputs
        required := e.RequiredInputs()

        // Check for sensitive data
        sensitiveInputs := e.SensitiveInputs()
        sensitiveOutputs := e.SensitiveOutputs()
    }
}

docs.text:
• SPECIFICATION.md - Full process profile specification
  • Process Spec Examples - Built-in process spec examples
  • Security Analysis - Process-aware security rules

docs.title: Code Samples and cURL
docs.text:
A walkthrough shows each request in three ways: as HTTP, as a curl command, and as the code a developer writes to send or handle it. PIDL generates the HTTP and cURL forms from a step's example. Code samples come from the implementations of the protocol, preferably from their tested source files, so the code a reader sees compiles and runs.

In the walkthrough viewer, each request and response panel has a tab for HTTP, cURL and every sample language. The reader's choice is kept from step to step; a step without that form shows HTTP with the tab disabled.

docs.title: cURL
docs.text:
Every example request gets an equivalent curl command: the method, the URL, each header in written order, and the body as it goes on the wire. You write nothing for it.

curl 'https://api.example/reports' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJ0eXAiOiJhdCtqd3Qi…'
  • Body. A body is written as JSON for readability. On the wire it is compact JSON with keys in the order written, which is also what a Content-Digest in the example covers. A body written as a JSON string is sent as the string's contents, for media types that are not JSON, such as a form.
  • Signed requests. curl cannot create HTTP message signatures, so the command for a signed request replays the example's signature headers, and a comment at the top says so.

docs.title: Code Samples
docs.text:
A sample is code in one language for one step:

Field Meaning language The highlighter name, such as go, typescript, python or csharp. Not http or curl, which PIDL generates label Tells samples in one language apart, such as the client's code and the API's role The entity whose developer writes this code code Inline code source Where the code lives: repo, optional ref (a tag or commit), path inside the repository with forward slashes, and region

A step where nothing goes over HTTP, such as a person approving in a browser, can still show code: the servers and the client run code for it.

Samples can live in two places:

  • A sample set, a file kept by an implementation, beside its tested code. The protocol document then names no implementation, and each SDK keeps its own samples current. Use this for a protocol with several implementations, or a protocol document shared across projects.
  • Inline in the document, on a step's example. Use this for a protocol and its one implementation in one repository.

docs.title: Sample Sets
docs.text:
A sample set attaches samples to steps by their address. Give the steps you want to show code for an id:

{
  "format": "pidl-samples/v1",
  "protocol": "oauth2-api-access",
  "name": "example-sdk-go",
  "samples": [
    {"step": "authorization-code/token-request", "language": "go", "label": "Client", "role": "client",
     "source": {"repo": "example.com/sdk", "path": "walkthrough/token_test.go", "region": "authorization-code.token-request"}},
    {"step": "call-api/api-request", "language": "go", "label": "Client", "role": "client",
     "source": {"repo": "example.com/sdk", "path": "walkthrough/api_test.go", "region": "call-api.request"}}
  ]
}
  • Addresses name a step as written: <scenario>/<step-id>, including a step of a fragment, which then shows wherever the fragment is included; <scenario> for samples about the whole scenario; or <step-id> in a document without scenarios.
  • protocol names the document's protocol ID, so a set is not joined to another protocol by mistake.
  • name names the implementation; a step without an example gets one citing it.

Join one or more sets to the document when generating, one per implementation:

pidl generate -f viewer --samples sdk-go.pidl-samples.json --samples sdk-ts.pidl-samples.json -o api.html api.json

An address that names no step, or a sample that is not resolved, is an error, so a set cannot fall silently behind the protocol. The format's schema is schema/samples.schema.json.

docs.title: Inline Samples
docs.text:
Put samples on a flow's example:

{
  "id": "api-request",
  "from": "client", "to": "api", "action": "api_request",
  "example": {
    "source": "RFC 6750 §2.1",
    "kind": "draft",
    "request": {"method": "GET", "url": "https://api.example/reports"},
    "samples": [
      {"language": "go", "label": "Client", "role": "client",
       "source": {"repo": "example.com/sdk", "ref": "v1.2.0",
                  "path": "walkthrough/api_test.go", "region": "call-api.request"}},
      {"language": "python", "label": "Client", "role": "client",
       "code": "res = client.get(\"https://api.example/reports\")"}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Code from Tested Files
docs.text:
Inline code drifts from the library it calls. A source points at a region of a real file instead, ideally a test that runs in that project's CI, so every sample compiles and runs with each release of the code it shows.

Mark the region with pidl:begin and pidl:end comments, in any comment syntax:

func TestCallAPI(t *testing.T) {
    // ...setup...

    // pidl:begin call-api.request
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, apiURL+"/reports", nil)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token.AccessToken)
    // pidl:end call-api.request
}

The sample is the code between the markers. Marker lines of other regions inside it are dropped, the common indentation is removed, and blank lines at either end are trimmed. Naming regions after the step they show keeps the two easy to match.

docs.title: Resolving and Checking
docs.text:
Generation never reads the source repositories or the network. It reads code recorded beforehand:

# A sample set records the code and its SHA-256 in the set itself
pidl samples resolve sdk-go.pidl-samples.json

# A document records them in a lock file beside it, api.samples.json
pidl samples resolve api.json

# Fail when a source is not resolved, its region is gone, or its code changed
pidl samples check sdk-go.pidl-samples.json
pidl samples check api.json

resolve reads each repository from a checkout at <root>/<repo>, where the root is --root, or $GOPATH/src (~/go/src) by default. --repo-dir <dir> reads every source from one checkout instead, which suits a sample set in the repository it describes. With a ref, a file is read as it is at that tag or commit.

In an implementation's CI, check its set against the protocol document, so a renamed or removed step is caught:

pidl samples check --repo-dir . --protocol api.json sdk-go.pidl-samples.json

When the code a sample shows changes on purpose, run pidl samples resolve again and commit the result.

docs.title: Narration for a Representation
docs.text: A step's narration describes the protocol, but a reader looking at the Go tab may want to hear about the code. A step's representations override its narration for http, curl or a sample language. See Narration.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Walkthrough Viewer
  • Narration

  • CLI Reference: samples

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Most protocols have more than one journey through the same roles. OAuth has several grants; AAuth has five access modes, from agent identity to federated authorization. Scenarios let one PIDL file describe all of them with one shared list of roles, so every diagram, table and outline generated from the file shows roles and journeys in the same order.

The built-in oauth2_api_access example is used throughout this page:

pidl scenarios oauth2_api_access

#   ID                       NAME                           KIND      STEPS  PARTICIPANTS
User-delegated access
1   authorization-code       Authorization code with PKCE   main          8  user, client, as, api
Service access
2   client-credentials       Client credentials             main          2  client, as, api
3   scope-challenge          Client credentials after a ... variant       4  client, as, api
4   async-export             Asynchronous export            main          5  client, as, api
5   signed-request           Signed request                 main          2  client, api
Fragments
6   client-token             Client credentials token       fragment      2  client, as
7   call-api                 Call the API                   fragment      2  client, api

docs.title: Writing Scenarios
docs.text:
Replace the top-level flows array with a scenarios array. Each scenario has an id, a name and its own flows:

{
  "entities": [
    {"id": "person", "name": "Person", "type": "user"},
    {"id": "agent", "name": "Agent", "type": "agent"},
    {"id": "resource", "name": "Resource", "type": "resource_server"},
    {"id": "ps", "name": "Person Server", "type": "authorization_server"}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "id": "agent-identity",
      "name": "Agent identity",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "signed_request"},
        {"from": "resource", "to": "agent", "action": "ok", "mode": "response"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Order Comes from the File
docs.text:
Order is never set with numbers. It comes from where things sit in the file:

  • Roles follow the entities array. Diagram columns, tables and outlines all use it. To change the column order of every diagram, move the entity.
  • Scenarios follow the scenarios array, arranged by group when the file declares groups, with variants after their base and fragments last.
  • Steps follow each scenario's flows array.

A scenario's participants list chooses which roles appear. It never reorders them, and validation reports a list that is out of entities order.

docs.title: Sections, Variants and Step IDs
docs.text:
A complete protocol has many scenarios. Groups put them in sections, variants pair alternative forms of one journey, and step IDs give each step a name that links, samples and narration can rely on:

{
  "groups": [
    {"id": "identity", "name": "Agent identity"},
    {"id": "access", "name": "Access modes"}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {"id": "agent-identity", "name": "Agent identity", "group": "identity", "flows": [
      {"id": "sign", "from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "signed_request"},
      {"id": "ok", "from": "resource", "to": "agent", "action": "response", "mode": "response"}
    ]},
    {"id": "agent-identity-approval", "name": "Agent identity with approval", "group": "identity",
     "variant_of": "agent-identity", "variant_label": "With user approval", "flows": [ ... ]},
    {"id": "ps-authorization", "name": "PS authorization", "group": "access", "flows": [
      {"id": "request", "from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "request"},
      {"id": "consent", "include": "consent"}
    ]}
  ]
}
  • Groups set the order of sections. pidl scenarios lists scenarios under their group's name, and --all-scenarios numbers files in the same order.
  • Variants follow their base and share its group. Viewers show a variant as a toggle on its base's entry.
  • Step IDs are unique within a scenario. A step inside an included fragment is addressed as <include>.<id>, for example consent.approve, so #ps-authorization/consent.approve links to that step in the viewer even after steps are added before it.

docs.title: Shared Steps: Fragments and Includes
docs.text:
Steps that several scenarios share, such as obtaining a token or asking the person for consent, go in a fragment: a scenario with "fragment": true. Other scenarios insert it with an include step:

{
  "id": "ps-authorization",
  "name": "PS authorization (three-party)",
  "flows": [
    {"include": "agent-token"},
    {"include": "person-token"},
    {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "authorize"},
    {"include": "consent"}
  ]
}

Diagrams draw an include as a labeled box across the fragment's participants. Use --expand to show the fragment's steps in place instead.

docs.title: Generating Output
docs.text:
# One scenario
pidl generate -f mermaid --scenario client-credentials oauth2_api_access

# One scenario with fragments shown step by step
pidl generate -f mermaid --scenario client-credentials --expand oauth2_api_access

# Every main scenario: 01-authorization-code.svg, 02-client-credentials.svg, ...
pidl generate -f svg --all-scenarios -o diagrams/ oauth2_api_access

# Add the fragments after the main scenarios: ... 06-client-token.svg
pidl generate -f svg --all-scenarios --include-fragments -o diagrams/ oauth2_api_access

File numbers match the # column of pidl scenarios, so a sorted file listing, a slide deck and the scenario list agree.

Some outputs describe the whole file rather than one scenario:

Format Output scenario-matrix Markdown table of roles by scenario. ● takes part directly, ○ takes part only through an included fragment token-table Markdown table of tokens: issuer, audience, binding, who checks each token, which claims they rely on, and the scenarios that issue and check it outline Markdown outline of roles, scenarios with numbered steps, and tokens, as a starting point for guides and slide decks outline-json The same outline as JSON, for deck and guide tooling 
pidl generate -f scenario-matrix oauth2_api_access
pidl generate -f outline -o api-outline.md oauth2_api_access

simulate and debug take --scenario and run the scenario with fragments expanded.

docs.title: Recording Who Checks What
docs.text:
Token definitions can list who checks each token and which claims they rely on. Flow security can say which tokens a step issues and checks, and who signs the request:

{
  "metadata": {
    "tokens": [
      {
        "id": "resource_token",
        "issuer": "resource",
        "verified_by": ["ps", "as"],
        "claims": [
          {"name": "agent_jkt", "checked_by": ["ps", "as"],
           "description": "Thumbprint of the agent's key, compared with the key that signed the request"}
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

{"from": "resource", "to": "agent", "action": "challenge", "mode": "response",
 "security": {"issues": ["resource_token"]}}

{"from": "ps", "to": "as", "action": "federate",
 "security": {"requires": ["signature"], "verifies": ["resource_token"]}}

With these fields, pidl analyze follows each token through a scenario:

Rule Reports SEC017 A role that no flow uses SEC018 A step that checks a token before any earlier step issues it SEC019 A request signed by someone other than its sender, or than the entity the presented token was delivered to SEC020 A receiver that checks a token without being listed in its verified_by SEC021 A fragment that no scenario includes

In the oauth2_api_access example, SEC019 flags the token request of the authorization code grant: the client presents an authorization code that was delivered to the user's browser, the interception that PKCE defends against.

pidl analyze oauth2_api_access                                   # whole file
pidl analyze --scenario authorization-code oauth2_api_access    # one scenario

docs.title: Composing Files
docs.text:
extends and imports understand scenarios:

  • extends keeps the base file's scenario order. A scenario with the same id in the derived file replaces the base one in place; new scenarios follow. exclude_scenarios removes base scenarios.
  • imports can bring in selected scenarios with "scenarios": ["id", ...]. The fragments they include come with them, and alias prefixes every ID they reference.
  • When composition leaves a file with both top-level flows and scenarios, the flows become the first scenario, named after the protocol.

docs.title: Comparing Versions
docs.text:
pidl diff matches scenarios by id. It reports scenarios that were added, removed or renamed, changed steps within each scenario, include steps that point at a different fragment, and roles or scenarios that moved relative to each other.

pidl diff aauth-draft-10.json aauth-draft-11.json

docs.title: In Go
docs.text:
p, err := pidl.ParseFile("aauth.json")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
for _, s := range p.ScenarioSummaries() {
    proj, err := p.Scenario(s.ID, pidl.ProjectOptions{})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    svg, err := render.RenderString(render.FormatSVG, proj)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    name := fmt.Sprintf("%02d-%s.svg", s.Position, s.ID)
    if err := os.WriteFile(name, []byte(svg), 0o600); err != nil {
        return err
    }
}

Protocol.Outline() returns the ordered outline as Go values, Protocol.Flatten() returns every scenario's flows once, and Protocol.TokenUsage(id) lists the scenarios that issue and check a token.

docs.title: Walkthrough Viewer
docs.text:
The walkthrough viewer turns a PIDL file into a page you can step through, one message at a time. It is built for learning a protocol and for presenting it: pick a scenario, press → and watch the active message, its two roles, and its request and response.

pidl generate -f viewer -o api.html oauth2_api_access
open api.html

The output is one self-contained HTML file. It needs no server and no network, so it can be emailed, attached to an issue or opened straight from disk.

To show walkthroughs inside other pages, such as a docs site, load the viewer from a CDN instead: see Embedding the Viewer.

docs.title: The Page
docs.text: Area Shows Menu bar The protocol name, a scenario selector (main scenarios, then shared steps), Overview, ← and →, and the step count Sequence card (left) The scenario's roles and steps. Shared steps (fragments) appear as labeled bands. The active step's arrow and label are highlighted, with its sender outlined in blue and its receiver in green; earlier steps are dimmed and later ones faint. Caption (under the diagram) The active step, the fragments it sits inside, its description and note, and any analyzer findings Request card (upper right) The active request, or the request a response answers Response card (lower right) The response, once you step to it

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Action → ↓ Space Page Down Next step ← ↑ Page Up Previous step Home Overview (all steps, none active) End Last step P Present on a 16:9 stage

The URL records the scenario and step, for example #federated-authorization/12, so a link opens at that step. A step with an ID can be linked by name instead, such as #ps-authorization/consent.approve, which keeps working when steps are added before it.

docs.title: Requests, Responses and Tokens
docs.text:
When a flow has an example, the cards show it:

  • HTTP: the request line, Host, headers in written order and body, or the status line, headers and body. Headers covered by the HTTP message signature (from Signature-Input) are marked signed. Long values such as JWTs shorten; click to expand.
  • cURL and code: the request as a generated curl command, and the step's code samples, one tab per language, titled by label and role, with a copy button. The tab you choose stays selected from step to step; a step without that form shows HTTP with the tab disabled.
  • Tokens: each decoded token's header and claims. Claims that the receiving role checks, according to the token's claims and checked_by, are highlighted.
  • Provenance: a draft badge for examples taken from the cited source with values aligned, or derived for examples written from its normative text, with the source section and the example's note.

A request's response appears only when you reach it, so the walkthrough reveals each answer in order. A pending response pairs with the poll it answers.

docs.title: Presenting
docs.text: Present (or P) places the page on a fixed 1600×900 stage scaled to the window, letterboxed, so it looks the same on any projector or shared screen. Theme cycles auto, light and dark.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The viewer reads a walkthrough (pidl-walkthrough/v1), the format pidl generate -f walkthrough-json produces: every scenario with fragments expanded, each step's example, and analyzer findings attached to the steps they concern (SEC016, flow provenance, is left out). Use that format to build other viewers.

docs.title: Developing the Viewer
docs.text:
The viewer lives in viewer/ (Vite, React and TypeScript):

cd viewer
npm ci
npm run data       # write public/walkthrough.json from the oauth2_api_access example
npm run dev        # http://localhost:5173
npm test
npm run build:embed  # rebuild render/viewer/viewer.html for the Go binary
npm run build:lib    # build the embeddable viewer into dist-lib/

go generate ./render runs the same build. CI fails when the committed render/viewer/viewer.html does not match a fresh build.

docs.title: Workflow Engine Exports
docs.text: PIDL process specifications can be exported to workflow orchestration platforms for execution. This guide covers the available exporters and how to use them.

docs.title: Supported Platforms
docs.text: Platform Language Export Format Use Case Temporal Go .go Durable workflow orchestration Prefect Python .py Data pipeline orchestration BPMN 2.0 XML .bpmn Standard interchange format AWS Step Functions JSON .json Serverless workflow orchestration

docs.title: Go Library Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl/export"

// Load your process specification
p, _ := pidl.ParseFile("pipeline.pidl.json")

// Export to Temporal
temporal := export.NewTemporalExporter()
goCode, _ := temporal.Export(p)

// Export to Prefect
prefect := export.NewPrefectExporter()
pythonCode, _ := prefect.Export(p)

// Export to BPMN
bpmn := export.NewBPMNExporter()
xml, _ := bpmn.Export(p)

// Export to AWS Step Functions
stepfn := export.NewStepFunctionsExporter()
asl, _ := stepfn.Export(p)

docs.title: Temporal Export
docs.text: The Temporal exporter generates Go code with workflow and activity stubs.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
exporter := export.NewTemporalExporter()
exporter.PackageName = "myworkflow"      // Go package name
exporter.WorkflowName = "ProcessData"    // Override workflow function name
exporter.IncludeActivities = true        // Generate activity stubs

docs.title: Generated Code Structure
docs.text:
// Code generated by PIDL. DO NOT EDIT.
package workflow

import (
    "context"
    "time"
    "go.temporal.io/sdk/activity"
    "go.temporal.io/sdk/workflow"
)

func ProcessDataWorkflow(ctx workflow.Context, input interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    ao := workflow.ActivityOptions{
        StartToCloseTimeout: 10 * time.Minute,
        RetryPolicy: &temporal.RetryPolicy{
            MaximumAttempts: 3,
        },
    }
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, ao)
    // ... workflow logic
}

// Activities with step-type-specific patterns
func ExtractDataActivity(ctx context.Context, input interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    // External service call pattern for "external" step type
    return input, nil
}

func TransformDataActivity(ctx context.Context, input interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    // LLM processing pattern for "llm" step type
    return input, nil
}

docs.title: Step Type Mapping
docs.text: PIDL Step Type Temporal Pattern deterministic Standard activity with deterministic logic llm Activity with LLM API call pattern human Signal-based human approval pattern external HTTP/API call with error handling tool Tool/function invocation pattern

docs.title: Prefect Export
docs.text: The Prefect exporter generates Python code with async/sync flow and task definitions.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
exporter := export.NewPrefectExporter()
exporter.FlowName = "process_data"  // Override flow function name
exporter.IncludeTasks = true        // Generate task stubs
exporter.UseAsync = true            // Generate async functions (default)

docs.title: Generated Code Structure
docs.text:
"""
process_data_flow - Generated by PIDL
Source: etl-pipeline
"""

from prefect import flow, task
import asyncio
from typing import Any, Dict

@task(name="Extract Data", tags=["external"])
async def extract_data_task(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Extract data from source."""
    # External service call pattern
    return data

@task(name="Transform Data", tags=["llm"])
async def transform_data_task(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Transform data using LLM."""
    # LLM processing pattern
    return data

@flow(name="process_data_flow")
async def process_data_flow(input_data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    ETL Pipeline
    Generated from PIDL process specification: etl-pipeline
    """
    result = input_data
    result = await extract_data_task(result)
    result = await transform_data_task(result)
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(process_data_flow({}))

docs.title: Sync Mode
docs.text:
For synchronous flows:

exporter := export.NewPrefectExporter()
exporter.UseAsync = false

This generates standard def functions instead of async def.

docs.title: BPMN 2.0 Export
docs.text: The BPMN exporter generates standard BPMN 2.0 XML for use with workflow engines like Camunda, Activiti, or for import into modeling tools.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
exporter := export.NewBPMNExporter()
exporter.ProcessID = "my-process"       // Override process ID
exporter.ProcessName = "My Process"     // Override process name

docs.title: Generated XML Structure
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<definitions xmlns="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL"
             xmlns:bpmndi="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/DI">
  <process id="etl-pipeline" name="ETL Pipeline" isExecutable="true">
    <startEvent id="start" name="Start"/>

    <serviceTask id="extract" name="Extract Data">
      <documentation>Extract data from source</documentation>
    </serviceTask>

    <serviceTask id="transform" name="Transform Data">
      <documentation>Transform using LLM</documentation>
    </serviceTask>

    <endEvent id="end" name="End"/>

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="start" targetRef="extract"/>
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="extract" targetRef="transform"/>
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="transform" targetRef="end"/>
  </process>
</definitions>

docs.title: Step Type Mapping
docs.text: PIDL Step Type BPMN Element deterministic <serviceTask> llm <serviceTask> with AI annotation human <userTask> external <serviceTask> tool <serviceTask>

docs.title: AWS Step Functions Export
docs.text: The Step Functions exporter generates Amazon States Language (ASL) JSON for AWS Step Functions.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
exporter := export.NewStepFunctionsExporter()
exporter.StateMachineName = "MyPipeline"  // Override name
exporter.Comment = "Data processing"       // Add comment
exporter.TimeoutSeconds = 3600             // State machine timeout

docs.title: Generated JSON Structure
docs.text:
{
  "Comment": "Generated from PIDL: ETL Pipeline",
  "StartAt": "extract",
  "States": {
    "extract": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::http:invoke",
      "Comment": "Extract data from source",
      "Next": "transform"
    },
    "transform": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel",
      "Comment": "Transform using LLM",
      "Next": "load",
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 1,
          "MaxAttempts": 3,
          "BackoffRate": 2.0
        }
      ]
    },
    "load": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Comment": "Load to database",
      "End": true
    }
  },
  "TimeoutSeconds": 3600
}

docs.title: Step Type to AWS Resource Mapping
docs.text: PIDL Step Type AWS Resource ARN deterministic arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke llm arn:aws:states:::bedrock:invokeModel human arn:aws:states:::activity:HumanReview external arn:aws:states:::http:invoke tool arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
PIDL parallel blocks are converted to Step Functions Parallel states:

{
  "parallel_block": {
    "Type": "Parallel",
    "Branches": [
      {
        "StartAt": "branch_a",
        "States": { "branch_a": { "Type": "Task", "End": true } }
      },
      {
        "StartAt": "branch_b",
        "States": { "branch_b": { "Type": "Task", "End": true } }
      }
    ],
    "Next": "join_step"
  }
}

docs.title: 1. Define Step Types
docs.text:
Always set step_type on process entities for accurate export:

{
  "id": "validate",
  "name": "Validate Input",
  "step_type": "deterministic"
}

docs.title: 2. Add Retry Strategies
docs.text:
Configure retry behavior in PIDL for it to be reflected in exports:

{
  "id": "api_call",
  "step_type": "external",
  "retry_strategy": {
    "max_attempts": 3,
    "initial_delay": "1s",
    "backoff_multiplier": 2.0
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Set Timeouts
docs.text:
Define processing timeouts for proper timeout handling:

{
  "id": "llm_step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "processing": {
    "timeout": "300s"
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Use Descriptive Names
docs.text:
Entity names become activity/task names in generated code:

{
  "id": "extract_customer_data",
  "name": "Extract Customer Data from CRM"
}

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Generated code contains stubs that need implementation
  • Parallel blocks require manual configuration in some platforms
  • Complex conditional logic may need manual adjustment
  • Human approval patterns vary by platform

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Process Specifications - Process spec fundamentals
  • Cost Tracking - Execution cost analysis
  • Data Lineage - Data flow tracking

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: pidl <command> [options] [arguments]

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Description validate Validate PIDL JSON files generate Generate diagrams from PIDL files scenarios List the scenarios in a PIDL file samples Resolve and check code samples from source repositories roles List protocol roles components List deployment components trust List trust relationships examples List or show built-in examples init Create a new PIDL file from template simulate Run protocol simulation with state tracking diff Compare two protocols and show differences debug Interactive step-through protocol debugger analyze Security analysis with attack surface detection resolve Resolve protocol imports and inheritance version Print version information help Show help message

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
Validate PIDL JSON files for correctness.

pidl validate [options] <file> [file...]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description -q Quiet mode (only show errors)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Validate single file
pidl validate protocol.json

# Validate multiple files
pidl validate *.json

# Quiet mode
pidl validate -q protocol.json

docs.title: generate
docs.text:
Generate diagrams from PIDL files.

pidl generate [options] <file>

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description Default -f Output format plantuml -o Output file, or directory with --all-scenarios stdout --scenario Scenario to render (required for files with scenarios, except whole-file formats) --expand Show included fragments step by step instead of as boxes false --all-scenarios Render every main scenario to NN-<id><ext> in the -o directory false --include-fragments With --all-scenarios, also render fragments after the main scenarios false --resolve Resolve imports and extends before generating false --samples Samples for walkthrough-json and viewer: the document's lock file or a sample set. Can be repeated <file without .json>.samples.json, when present --client Postman: the role whose requests are sent the first agent or client entity --mock Postman: save example responses for a mock server and check only status codes false --signer Postman: proxy sends requests with HTTP message signatures through a signing proxy --targets Postman environments: a JSON file naming each target's role URLs and signer --target Postman environments: the target in --targets to write

docs.title: Formats
docs.text: Format Description plantuml PlantUML sequence diagram mermaid Mermaid sequence diagram mermaid-state Mermaid state diagram (requires entity states) mermaid-component Mermaid deployment component diagram mermaid-trust Mermaid trust relationship diagram markdown-matrix Markdown protocol role matrix dot Graphviz DOT data flow d2 D2 sequence diagram d2-flow D2 data flow diagram d2-arch D2 architecture diagram svg, svg-animated SVG sequence diagram, optionally with animated flow dots svg-network Network boundary diagram svg-component, svg-trust SVG deployment component and trust relationship diagrams infographic Compact SVG for LinkedIn and datasheets scenario-matrix Markdown table of roles by scenario (whole file) token-table Markdown table of tokens, checkers and claims (whole file) outline Markdown outline of roles, scenarios and tokens (whole file) outline-json The outline as JSON (whole file) walkthrough-json A walkthrough (pidl-walkthrough/v1): expanded scenarios with examples and findings, for viewers (whole file) viewer Self-contained HTML walkthrough viewer (whole file) postman Postman collection: a folder per scenario, chained requests and checks (whole file) postman-environment Postman environment for one target in a --targets file

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# One scenario of a multi-scenario file
pidl generate -f mermaid --scenario client-credentials oauth2_api_access

# Every scenario, numbered in file order
pidl generate -f svg --all-scenarios -o diagrams/ oauth2_api_access

# Step-by-step walkthrough viewer in one HTML file
pidl generate -f viewer -o api.html oauth2_api_access

# Postman collection that sends signed requests through a signing proxy
pidl generate -f postman --signer proxy -o api.postman_collection.json oauth2_api_access

# Viewer with the code samples of two implementations
pidl generate -f viewer --samples sdk-go.pidl-samples.json --samples sdk-ts.pidl-samples.json -o api.html api.json

# PlantUML to stdout
pidl generate protocol.json

# Mermaid to file
pidl generate -f mermaid -o diagram.mmd protocol.json

# D2 sequence diagram
pidl generate -f d2 protocol.json

# D2 architecture diagram
pidl generate -f d2-arch protocol.json

# From built-in example
pidl generate oauth2_authorization_code

docs.title: scenarios
docs.text:
List the scenarios in a PIDL file: main scenarios in file order, then fragments. The # column matches the file numbers written by generate --all-scenarios --include-fragments.

pidl scenarios [options] <file>

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description Default -f Output format: table, json table

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
pidl scenarios oauth2_api_access
pidl scenarios -f json oauth2_api_access

See the Scenarios guide.

docs.title: samples
docs.text:
Resolve and check code samples whose code comes from marked regions of files in source repositories.

pidl samples <resolve|check> [options] <file>

<file> is a document whose steps carry samples, or a sample set (pidl-samples/v1). resolve reads every sample source and records the code and its SHA-256: for a document in a lock file beside it, for a sample set in the set itself. check fails when a source is not resolved, its region is missing, or its code changed since it was resolved; run it in CI.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description Default --root Directory holding repository checkouts at <root>/<repo> $GOPATH/src, or ~/go/src --lock A document's lock file <file without .json>.samples.json --repo-dir Read every source from this checkout instead of <root>/<repo>, such as the repository a sample set lives in --protocol With a sample set, also check that every step address names a step of this document

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Write a document's lock file
pidl samples resolve api.json

# Resolve an implementation's sample set from its own checkout
pidl samples resolve --repo-dir . sdk-go.pidl-samples.json

# In the implementation's CI: fail when a sample fell behind its source
# or names a step the protocol no longer has

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
    "github.com/grokify/pidl/render"
    "github.com/grokify/pidl/examples"
)

func main() {
    // Load built-in example
    p, err := examples.GetProtocol("oauth2_pkce")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    // Validate
    if errs := p.Validate(); errs.HasErrors() {
        log.Fatal(errs)
    }

    // Generate Mermaid diagram
    r := render.NewMermaid()
    r.Autonumber = true

    diagram, err := r.RenderString(p)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    fmt.Println(diagram)
}

docs.title: Protocol Simulation
docs.text:
// Create executor
executor := pidl.NewExecutor(protocol)

// Optional: custom condition evaluator
executor.ConditionEvaluator = func(ctx *pidl.ExecutionContext, flow *pidl.Flow) bool {
    return true // evaluate condition
}

// Execute full protocol
trace, err := executor.Execute()

// Step-by-step execution
ctx := executor.NewContext()
for !ctx.Completed {
    step, err := executor.Step(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        break
    }
    fmt.Printf("Step %d: %s -> %s\n", step.StepNumber, step.From, step.To)
}

// Access trace
fmt.Println(trace.String())
jsonBytes, _ := trace.ToJSON()

docs.title: Interactive Debugger
docs.text:
// Create debug session
session := pidl.NewDebugSession(protocol)

// Set breakpoints
session.SetBreakpoint(3, "")                    // Unconditional
session.SetBreakpoint(5, "client.state == \"waiting\"") // Conditional

// Step through execution
step, _ := session.Step()
fmt.Printf("Executed: %s\n", step.Action)

// Continue until breakpoint
session.Continue()

// Inspect state
state := session.Inspect()
fmt.Printf("Flow %d, Completed: %v\n", state.FlowIndex, state.IsCompleted)
fmt.Printf("Entity states: %v\n", state.EntityStates)

// Inspect specific entity
entity, entityState, _ := session.InspectEntity("client")
fmt.Printf("%s is in state: %s\n", entity.Name, entityState)

// Modify state
session.SetEntityState("client", "authenticated")

// Reset and restart
session.Reset()

// List flows with markers
fmt.Println(session.FormatFlowList())

docs.title: Security Analysis
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl/analyze"

// Run analysis with default options
analysis := analyze.Analyze(protocol, analyze.DefaultAnalysisOptions())

// Custom options
opts := analyze.AnalysisOptions{
    MinSeverity:   analyze.SeverityMedium,
    Categories:    []analyze.RiskCategory{analyze.CategoryAuthentication},
    DisabledRules: []string{"SEC008"},
}
analysis = analyze.Analyze(protocol, opts)

// Check results
if analysis.HasRisks() {
    fmt.Println(analysis.String())
}

if analysis.HasRisksAtOrAbove(analyze.SeverityHigh) {
    // Critical action needed
}

// Filter risks
authRisks := analysis.RisksByCategory(analyze.CategoryAuthentication)
highRisks := analysis.RisksBySeverity(analyze.SeverityHigh)

// Output formats
fmt.Println(analysis.ToMarkdown())
jsonBytes, _ := analysis.ToJSON()

// Access summary
fmt.Printf("Score: %d/100, Total: %d risks\n",
    analysis.Summary.Score, analysis.Summary.TotalRisks)
