docs.title: Walkthrough Format
docs.text:
PIDL has two formats:

PIDL Walkthrough Written by people pidl generate -f walkthrough-json Holds roles, scenarios and flows, with extends, includes and sample references every scenario with fragments expanded in place, cURL commands rendered, code samples resolved and analyzer findings attached Read by the pidl tools the walkthrough viewer, and any tool that presents a protocol step by step Schema schema/pidl.schema.json schema/walkthrough.schema.json

A walkthrough is self-contained: a reader needs none of PIDL's include, ordering, resolution or analysis rules. This page describes version 1, pidl-walkthrough/v1.

docs.title: Producing a Walkthrough
docs.text:
pidl generate -f walkthrough-json -o api.walkthrough.json oauth2_api_access

From Go, render.NewWalkthroughJSON().Render(w, protocol) writes the same JSON, and protocol.Walkthrough(findings) returns it as a pidl.Walkthrough.

Name walkthrough files <name>.walkthrough.json, so their format is clear without opening them.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
{
  "format": "pidl-walkthrough/v1",
  "id": "oauth2-api-access",
  "name": "OAuth 2.0 API Access",
  "language": "en-US",
  "roles": [{ "position": 1, "id": "person", "name": "Person" }],
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "position": 1,
      "id": "agent-identity",
      "name": "Agent identity",
      "participants": ["agent", "resource"],
      "steps": [
        { "number": 1, "from": "agent", "to": "resource", "label": "signed request", "location": "scenarios[0].flows[0] (agent-identity)" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Field Required Holds format yes pidl-walkthrough/v1 id, name yes the protocol's identifier and display name description what the protocol is for language yes the BCP 47 tag of the narration's source language pronunciations how to speak terms, by term and language roles yes the participants, in display order groups navigation sections scenarios are listed under scenarios yes the scenarios, in navigation order tokens token definitions, with the claims each role checks findings analyzer findings that concern no single step

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Field Required Holds position, id, name yes order, identifier and display name participants yes the role IDs taking part, in display order steps yes the messages, with included fragments expanded in place fragment true for shared steps that other scenarios include group, variant_of, variant_label navigation: its group, and the scenario it is a variant of description, narration, briefing prose, spoken text by language, and an introduction samples code samples for the whole scenario

docs.title: Step
docs.text:
Field Required Holds number yes the 1-based position in the expanded scenario from, to, label yes sender, receiver and message name location yes where the flow is written in the PIDL file, such as scenarios[1].flows[0] (consent) id the flow ID, <include>.<id> inside a fragment response true for a response phase, fragments the phase, and the fragments the step sits inside, outermost first description, note, narration, representations prose, and spoken text by language, with overrides per representation (such as curl) signed_by, issues, verifies security: the signer, and the tokens issued and verified example the HTTP request or response, decoded tokens and code samples curl a cURL command equivalent to the example request findings analyzer findings about this step

The schema has every field, with descriptions.

docs.title: Versions and Compatibility
docs.text:
format names the major version. Within a major version:

  • New fields are optional, so every v1 walkthrough stays valid.
  • Readers ignore fields they do not know. The schema allows extra properties for this reason.
  • A field's type and meaning do not change.

Removing or renaming a field, changing its type or meaning, or making a field required starts a new major version, pidl-walkthrough/v2.

A reader accepts its own major version and refuses others with a message naming both. Walkthroughs written before the format had a version have no format field; read them as v1.

docs.title: Reading a Walkthrough
docs.text:
• Validate with any JSON Schema 2020-12 validator against schema/walkthrough.schema.json. In Go, the schema is embedded as schema.WalkthroughSchemaJSON.
  • TypeScript types generated from the schema are in viewer/src/walkthrough.gen.ts.
  • Treat the content as data. A walkthrough may come from anywhere, so render its text as text, never as HTML, and open only http: and https: links from it.

docs.title: Changing the Format
docs.text:
The Go types (pidl.Walkthrough) are the source. After changing them, regenerate the schema and the TypeScript types:

(cd schema/gen && go run .)
(cd viewer && npm run types)

CI fails when either file is out of date, and validates every built-in example against the schema.

docs.title: PIDL v0.1.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2025-04-18

This is the initial release of PIDL (Protocol Interaction Description Language), a JSON-based DSL for describing protocol choreography that compiles to diagrams.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Protocol Interaction Description Language - a JSON-based DSL for describing protocol choreography that compiles to diagrams
  • Support for OAuth 2.0, PKCE, OIDC, MCP, and A2A protocol examples
  • Three diagram output formats: PlantUML, Mermaid, and Graphviz DOT

docs.title: Core Library
docs.text:
• Protocol, Entity, Flow, and Phase types for modeling protocol interactions
  • JSON parser with ParseFile, Parse, and ParseReader functions
  • Comprehensive validation with detailed error reporting
  • High-level operations: ValidateFile, ValidateFiles, NewMinimalProtocol, WriteProtocolFile
  • JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for external validation tools

docs.title: Diagram Renderers
docs.text:
• PlantUML - Sequence diagram generation with phase groupings
  • Mermaid - Sequence diagram generation for web embedding
  • Graphviz DOT - Data flow diagram generation

docs.title: CLI Tool
docs.text:
go install github.com/grokify/pidl/cmd/pidl@latest

Commands:

  • pidl validate - Validate PIDL JSON files
  • pidl generate - Generate diagrams (PlantUML, Mermaid, DOT)
  • pidl examples - List or show built-in protocol examples
  • pidl init - Create new protocol files from templates

docs.title: Built-in Examples
docs.text: Example Protocol oauth2_authorization_code OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow oauth2_pkce OAuth 2.0 with PKCE oidc_authentication OpenID Connect Authentication mcp_tool_invocation MCP Tool Invocation a2a_agent_delegation A2A Agent Delegation

# List available examples
pidl examples

pidl generate oauth2_authorization_code

# Generate a Mermaid diagram
pidl generate -f mermaid oauth2_pkce

# Create a new protocol file
pidl init my-protocol.json

# Validate protocol files
pidl validate my-protocol.json

docs.title: PIDL v0.2.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2025-04-18

This release adds significant new features to PIDL including annotations, alternatives, conditions, notes, nested phases, and the D2 diagram format.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Add annotations, alternatives, conditions, notes, and nested phases to PIDL
  • Enhanced renderers with support for alt/else blocks, opt conditionals, and nested phase visualization
  • New D2 diagram format with sequence, flow, and architecture rendering styles
  • Comprehensive validation for phase hierarchies and new flow features

docs.title: D2 Diagram Renderer
docs.text:
A new diagram format with three rendering styles:

  • d2 / d2-sequence - Sequence diagram style
  • d2-flow - Data flow diagram style
  • d2-arch - Architecture diagram style
pidl generate -f d2 oauth2_pkce
pidl generate -f d2-arch mcp_tool_invocation

docs.title: Flow Extensions
docs.text:
New fields on Flow for richer protocol descriptions:

Field Description condition Conditional execution (renders as opt block) note Visible note in diagram annotations Typed metadata (security, performance, etc.) alternatives Alternative/error paths (renders as alt/else block)

docs.title: Annotation Types
docs.text:
Six built-in annotation types for flow metadata:

Type Use Case security Security considerations performance Performance notes deprecated Deprecation warnings info General information warning Warning messages error Error conditions

docs.title: Nested Phases
docs.text:
Phases can now have parent references for hierarchical grouping:

{
  "phases": [
    {"id": "auth", "name": "Authentication"},
    {"id": "mfa", "name": "MFA Challenge", "parent": "auth"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Alternative Paths
docs.text:
Model error handling and branching flows:

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "request",
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "condition": "error",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "error_response"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Mermaid
docs.text:
• opt blocks for conditional flows
  • alt/else blocks for alternatives
  • note right of for flow notes and annotations
  • Colored rect blocks for nested phases

docs.title: PlantUML
docs.text:
• opt/alt/else blocks for conditionals and alternatives
  • Colored box containers for nested phases
  • OpenIconic icons for annotation prefixes

docs.title: D2
docs.text:
• Condition label prefixes
  • Grouped alternatives
  • Nested phase groups with hierarchy support

docs.title: Graphviz DOT
docs.text:
• Condition edge labels
  • Alternative edges with distinct styling

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
New validation rules:

  • Phase parent reference validation with cycle detection
  • Annotation type and text validation
  • Alternative condition and flows validation
  • Entity reference validation in alternative flows

docs.text:
Release Date: 2025-05-18

This release introduces native SVG rendering capabilities including static sequence diagrams, animated flow visualizations with moving dots, and network boundary diagrams for security architecture visualization.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Native SVG rendering with static sequence diagrams, animated flow visualizations, and network boundary diagrams
  • CSS animation support with per-message control and semantic presets (request, success, error, warning, highlight)
  • Template system with 5 built-in styles: default, minimal, sketch, blueprint, dark
  • Network boundary diagrams for visualizing trust zones and security boundaries

docs.title: SVG Sequence Diagrams
docs.text:
Generate self-contained SVG sequence diagrams directly from PIDL:

# Static SVG sequence diagram
pidl generate -f svg oauth2_pkce

# Animated SVG with flow dots
pidl generate -f svg-animated oauth2_pkce

Features:

  • Light and dark theme support via --theme flag
  • CSS custom properties for easy styling
  • Print-friendly output with animation fallback

docs.title: Animated Flow Visualization
docs.text:
CSS-based animations show data flow with moving dots along message paths:

pidl generate -f svg-animated --theme=dark oauth2_pkce

Animation features:

  • offset-path CSS animations for smooth dot movement
  • Configurable duration, delay, and easing
  • Print media query disables animations automatically

docs.title: Per-Message Animation Control
docs.text:
Control animation on individual flows with the animation field:

{
  "flows": [
    {
      "from": "client",
      "to": "server",
      "action": "request",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": true,
        "preset": "request",
        "duration": "1.5s",
        "dot_color": "#3182ce"
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Semantic Animation Presets

docs.title: PIDL v0.4.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-06-28

This release introduces protocol composition, runtime execution simulation, protocol comparison, interactive debugging, and security analysis capabilities.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Protocol composition with imports and inheritance for modular protocol design
  • Runtime execution engine with state tracking and execution traces
  • Protocol comparison (diff) for detecting changes between protocols
  • Interactive step-through debugger with breakpoints and state inspection
  • Security analysis with 10 built-in attack surface detection rules

docs.title: Protocol Composition
docs.text:
Build modular protocols with imports and inheritance:

# Resolve imports and extends to output merged protocol
pidl resolve protocol-with-imports.json

Features:

  • Import entities and phases from other protocols with optional aliasing
  • Extend base protocols with exclusion filters
  • Standard library of common protocols (examples/stdlib/)
  • Circular import/extends detection
  • Automatic resolution in generate command

Example composition:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "my-oauth",
    "name": "My OAuth Extension"
  },
  "extends": {
    "path": "stdlib/oauth_entities.json",
    "exclude_phases": ["optional_refresh"]
  },
  "imports": [
    {
      "path": "stdlib/mcp_entities.json",
      "entities": ["mcp_client", "mcp_server"],
      "alias": "mcp"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Protocol Simulation
docs.text:
Run protocol simulations with state tracking:

# Run full simulation
pidl simulate protocol.json

# Verbose with step-by-step output
pidl simulate -v protocol.json

# Output trace as SVG
pidl simulate --trace-format=svg --trace-output=trace.svg protocol.json

# Output trace as JSON
pidl simulate -json protocol.json

Features:

  • Protocol execution engine with flow-by-flow processing
  • Entity state tracking with initial state initialization
  • Execution trace recording with timestamps
  • Conditional flow evaluation with custom evaluators
  • State mutation validation

docs.title: Protocol Comparison
docs.text:
Compare two protocols to detect changes:

# Compare protocols
pidl diff base.json updated.json

# Output as markdown
pidl diff -f markdown base.json updated.json

# Summary only
pidl diff -q base.json updated.json

Comparison detects:

  • Added, removed, and modified entities
  • Added, removed, and modified flows
  • Phase changes
  • Metadata differences

docs.title: Interactive Debugger
docs.text:
Step through protocol execution with breakpoints:

pidl debug protocol.json

Commands:

Command Description step, s Execute next flow continue, c Run until breakpoint or completion break <idx> [cond] Set breakpoint at flow index delete <idx> Remove breakpoint breakpoints List all breakpoints inspect Show current state inspect entity <id> Show entity details and state inspect flow <idx> Show flow details list List flows with position marker set <entity> <state> Set entity state reset Restart execution quit, q Exit debugger

Features:

  • Conditional breakpoints with state expressions
  • Entity state inspection and modification
  • Execution trace access
  • Flow listing with execution markers

docs.title: Security Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze protocols for security risks:

# Run security analysis
pidl analyze protocol.json

# Output as markdown
pidl analyze -f markdown -o security-report.md protocol.json

# Fail if high-severity risks found (for CI)
pidl analyze --fail-on=high protocol.json

# Filter by severity
pidl analyze --min-severity=high protocol.json

Built-in security rules:

Rule Severity Description SEC001 High Trust boundary violation (untrusted to trusted without security) SEC002 High Missing encryption on confidential flow SEC003 Medium Unbound bearer token (no mTLS/DPoP binding) SEC004 High Missing authentication on external flow SEC005 Medium JWT without defined audience SEC006 Medium Token transmitted in redirect SEC007 Medium Missing mTLS on sensitive flow SEC008 Low Entity without defined trust level SEC009 Medium Sensitive data in redirect parameters SEC010 Medium Weak authentication method

Output includes:

  • Risk details with location and remediation
  • Summary by severity and category
  • Security score (0-100)

docs.title: CLI Enhancements
docs.text:
New commands:

Command Description simulate Run protocol simulation with state tracking diff Compare two protocols debug Interactive step-through debugger analyze Security analysis resolve Resolve protocol imports and inheritance

New simulate options:

Flag Description -steps Maximum steps to execute -v Verbose output -json Output trace as JSON --trace-format Trace format: text, json, svg, mermaid --trace-output Write trace to file

docs.title: Go Library
docs.text:
New packages and types:

import (
    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
    "github.com/grokify/pidl/analyze"
)

// Protocol composition
resolved, err := pidl.ResolveProtocol(protocol, basePath)

// Execution
executor := pidl.NewExecutor(protocol)
trace, err := executor.Execute()

// Comparison
diff := pidl.Compare(base, updated, pidl.DiffOptions{})

// Debugging
session := pidl.NewDebugSession(protocol)
session.SetBreakpoint(3, "client.state == \"waiting\"")
step, _ := session.Step()

// Security analysis
analysis := analyze.Analyze(protocol, analyze.DefaultAnalysisOptions())
if analysis.HasRisksAtOrAbove(analyze.SeverityHigh) {
    // handle risks
}

docs.title: PIDL v0.5.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-07-12

This release introduces advanced process specification features, integrations, and new protocol examples. Major additions include data lineage tracking, parallel execution modeling, cost and latency budget tracking, JSON Schema validation, workflow engine exports, and integrations for MkDocs, GitHub Actions, and VS Code.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Process specifications for modeling workflows with step types and data ports
  • Data lineage tracking for tracing data flow through process steps
  • Parallel execution modeling with fork/join, race, and scatter/gather patterns
  • Cost and latency budget tracking with SLI analysis
  • JSON Schema validation for data ports with registry support
  • Workflow engine exports for Temporal, Prefect, BPMN, and AWS Step Functions
  • Infographic renderer with size presets and themes for social media
  • MkDocs plugin for rendering PIDL diagrams in documentation
  • GitHub Action for CI/CD validation
  • VS Code extension with syntax highlighting and live preview
  • New protocol examples: SAML 2.0, WebAuthn/FIDO2, SCIM

docs.title: Data Lineage Tracking
docs.text:
Track data flow through process specifications with lineage analysis:

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

// Analyze data lineage
lineage := pidl.AnalyzeDataLineage(protocol)

// Find upstream/downstream connections
upstream := lineage.GetUpstream("transform", "input")
downstream := lineage.GetDownstream("extract", "output")

// Impact analysis - what's affected if this entity changes?
impacted := lineage.GetImpactedEntities("transform")

// Data provenance - where does this entity's data come from?
sources := lineage.GetDataProvenance("load")

// Sensitive data path tracking
if lineage.HasSensitiveDataFlow() {
    for _, path := range lineage.SensitiveDataPaths {
        // Handle sensitive data paths
    }
}

Features:

  • Automatic port-to-port connection inference
  • Explicit data mappings via flow.data_mappings
  • Sensitive data path tracking
  • Impact analysis (downstream effects)
  • Provenance analysis (upstream sources)

docs.title: Parallel Execution Modeling
docs.text:
Model parallel execution patterns in process specifications:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "fork_point",
      "name": "Fork",
      "step_type": "parallel",
      "parallel": {
        "mode": "fork_join",
        "join_condition": "all",
        "branches": [
          {"id": "b1", "entity_id": "worker_1"},
          {"id": "b2", "entity_id": "worker_2"}
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze execution graph
graph := pidl.AnalyzeExecutionGraph(protocol)

// Get execution stages (parallelizable groups)
for _, stage := range graph.Stages {
    fmt.Printf("Stage %s: %v\n", stage.ID, stage.Steps)
}

// Find critical path
fmt.Println("Critical path:", graph.CriticalPath)

// Check if two entities can run in parallel
if pidl.CanExecuteInParallel(protocol, "stepA", "stepB") {
    // Execute concurrently
}

// Get maximum parallelism
maxParallel := pidl.GetMaxParallelism(protocol)

Parallel modes:

Mode Description fork_join Execute branches in parallel, wait for all race Execute branches in parallel, first wins scatter Distribute work across instances gather Collect results from parallel branches

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text:
Estimate and track execution costs for process specifications:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "llm_step",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "processing": {
        "cost_model": {
          "type": "token_based",
          "input_token_cost": 0.003,
          "output_token_cost": 0.015,
          "estimated_input_tokens": 1000,
          "estimated_output_tokens": 500,
          "cost_unit": "USD"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze process costs
analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessCosts(protocol)

// Total estimated cost
fmt.Printf("Expected cost: $%.4f\n", analysis.TotalEstimate.ExpectedCost)

// Cost by step type
for stepType, cost := range analysis.CostByType {
    fmt.Printf("%s: $%.4f\n", stepType, cost)
}

// Calculate actual execution cost
metrics := pidl.ExecutionMetrics{
    InputTokens:  1500,
    OutputTokens: 750,
    Duration:     30 * time.Second,
}
actualCost := pidl.CalculateExecutionCost(entity, metrics)

Cost model types:

Type Description fixed Fixed cost per execution token_based Cost based on input/output tokens time_based Cost based on execution duration api_call Cost per API call hybrid Combined cost factors

docs.title: Latency Budget Tracking
docs.text:
Define timing SLIs (Service Level Indicators) for process steps:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "llm_step",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "processing": {
        "latency_budget": {
          "p50": "2s",
          "p95": "8s",
          "p99": "15s",
          "max": "30s",
          "variance_class": "high"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze process latency
analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessLatency(protocol)

// Total latency estimates
fmt.Printf("P50: %s, P95: %s, P99: %s\n",
    analysis.TotalLatency.P50,
    analysis.TotalLatency.P95,
    analysis.TotalLatency.P99)

// Critical path latency
fmt.Printf("Critical path: %v\n", analysis.CriticalPath)
fmt.Printf("Critical path P50: %s\n", analysis.CriticalPathLatency.P50)

// Parallel savings
fmt.Printf("Parallel savings: %s\n", analysis.ParallelSavings)

// Budget violations
for _, v := range analysis.BudgetViolations {
    fmt.Printf("%s: %s exceeded (budget: %s, estimated: %s)\n",
        v.EntityID, v.Metric, v.Budget, v.Estimated)
}

// Measure actual execution
measurement := pidl.CalculateActualLatency(entity, 5*time.Second)
if measurement.ExceedsP95 {
    // Handle SLI violation
}

Variance classes:

Class Description low Consistent, predictable latency (deterministic steps) medium Moderate variance (external APIs, tools) high High variance (LLM, human tasks)

docs.title: JSON Schema Validation
docs.text:
Validate data port inputs and outputs against JSON Schema:

// Create schema registry
registry := pidl.NewSchemaRegistry()
registry.SetBasePath("./schemas")

// Load and cache schemas
schema, _ := registry.LoadSchema("user.schema.json")

// Validate data against schema
result := pidl.ValidateData(data, schema)
if !result.Valid {
    for _, err := range result.Errors {
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", err.Path, err.Message)
    }
}

// Validate entity inputs
validator := pidl.NewPortSchemaValidator()
validator.SetBasePath("./schemas")

result, _ := validator.ValidateEntityInputs(entity, inputs)
if !result.Valid {
    fmt.Println(result.Error())
}

Supported validations:

  • Type checking (string, number, integer, boolean, array, object, null)
  • Required fields
  • Enum constraints
  • Min/max for numbers
  • MinLength/maxLength for strings
  • Nested object validation
  • Array item validation

docs.title: Workflow Engine Exports

Export PIDL process specifications to workflow orchestration platforms:

docs.title: PIDL v0.6.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-09-13

This release adds flow verification provenance for incident attack-flows — a way to record how well-substantiated each step is and where it is sourced from — along with renderer badges and an analyzer rule, plus a comprehensive AIDLC workflow process-specification example.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Flow.Verification records evidentiary provenance: a verification tier, source, and citation
  • Verification tiers — reported, corroborated, reproduced, partially_reproduced — matching the aisecurity-incidents deepdive.json vocabulary
  • d2 and mermaid sequence renderers emit a per-flow provenance badge
  • A security-analysis rule flags flows below the corroborated tier
  • New comprehensive AIDLC workflow process-specification example

docs.title: Flow Verification Provenance
docs.text:
Record where an attack-flow step comes from and how well-substantiated it is:

{
  "from": "agent-collective",
  "to": "hugging-face",
  "action": "exploit_worker",
  "verification": {
    "tier": "corroborated",
    "source": "METR",
    "citation": "https://metr.org/..."
  }
}
  • VerificationTier — reported | corroborated | reproduced | partially_reproduced
  • FlowVerification { tier, source, citation } on Flow, with a Flow.HasVerification() helper
  • The schema addition is additive and backward-compatible

See the Flows guide and Specification.

docs.title: Renderer Provenance Badges
docs.text: d2 and mermaid sequence renderers emit a compact provenance badge per flow (e.g. 🔎 corroborated — METR), gated by SequenceRenderOptions.ShowVerification (on by default).

docs.title: Analyzer Rule
docs.text: A new security-analysis rule flags flows in agent/attack protocols that lack verification provenance at or above the corroborated tier — surfacing inferred or under-sourced steps in a published attack-flow.

docs.title: AIDLC Workflow Example
docs.text: A comprehensive AI Development Lifecycle (AIDLC) workflow process specification was added to the examples.

docs.title: PIDL v0.7.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-19

This release lets one PIDL file describe a whole protocol: its roles and an ordered list of scenarios, with shared steps written once as fragments. Every output follows the file's order, so diagrams, tables, outlines and the slide decks and guides built from them agree. It also brings the fixes prepared since v0.6.0: D2 sequence diagrams, deterministic SVG output, and Windows builds.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Scenarios: named journeys through the same roles, such as AAuth's five access modes, in one file
  • Fragments and include steps: shared steps drawn as labeled boxes in PlantUML, Mermaid, D2 and SVG, or expanded in place
  • Consistent ordering: the entities and scenarios arrays set the order of every output
  • Overview outputs: roles-by-scenario matrix, token table, and an ordered outline in Markdown and JSON
  • Token verification: record who checks each token and claim and who signs each request; new analyzer rules follow tokens through a scenario
  • AAuth example: draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11 with its five access modes

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
{
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "id": "ps-authorization",
      "name": "PS authorization (three-party)",
      "flows": [
        {"include": "person-token"},
        {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "authorize"},
        {"include": "consent"}
      ]
    },
    {"id": "consent", "name": "User consent", "fragment": true, "flows": [ ... ]}
  ]
}

A file has either flows, which works exactly as before, or scenarios. See the Scenarios guide and the specification.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: Command What it does pidl scenarios <file> Lists scenarios in output order generate --scenario <id> Renders one scenario generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> Writes 01-<id>.svg, 02-<id>.svg, … in file order generate --expand Shows included fragments step by step generate -f scenario-matrix Roles by scenario generate -f token-table Tokens, checkers, claims and the scenarios that use them generate -f outline / outline-json Ordered outline for guides and decks simulate, debug, analyze --scenario <id> Work on one scenario

docs.title: Token Verification and Analysis
docs.text:
Token definitions gain verified_by and claims; flow security gains signed_by, issues and verifies. New rules:

Rule Reports SEC017 A role that no flow uses SEC018 A token checked before any earlier step issues it SEC019 A request signed by someone other than its sender or the token holder SEC020 A token checked by an entity not in its verified_by SEC021 A fragment that no scenario includes

In the AAuth example, SEC019 flags federated access, where the PS signs the request to the AS while presenting a resource token delivered to the agent.

docs.title: Composition and Diff
docs.text: extends and imports merge scenarios, with exclude_scenarios and an import scenarios selector. pidl diff compares scenarios by ID and reports roles and scenarios that moved.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• Network boundary diagrams list entities in entities order instead of alphabetically. Sort the entities array to keep the previous layout.
  • Flow.sequence is deprecated. It is a display-only step number and never affected order.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• D2 sequence diagrams render messages as edges, with quoted labels and correct response direction
  • Network and trust SVG output, network boundary assignment and pidl diff output no longer depend on map iteration order
  • Labeled process flows link one output to one input instead of every input
  • Windows checkouts use LF line endings, so embedded SVG templates and golden tests match other platforms
  • CLI components and trust no longer crash without a metadata block; the debugger no longer loops at end of input

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Existing files need no changes. To adopt scenarios, move the top-level flows into a scenario:

{"scenarios": [{"id": "main", "name": "Main flow", "flows": [ ... ]}]}

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go install github.com/grokify/pidl/cmd/pidl@v0.7.0

docs.title: PIDL v0.8.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-19

This release turns a PIDL file into a walkthrough you can present. pidl generate -f viewer writes one self-contained HTML page that steps through each scenario one message at a time: the active roles and message are highlighted on the sequence diagram, a narrative explains the step, and the request and response appear beside it with their headers, bodies and decoded tokens. The page needs no server, so it can be shared as a file.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Walkthrough viewer for any PIDL protocol, with presentation controls and a 16:9 presentation mode
  • Flow examples: illustrative requests, responses and decoded tokens, each citing its source
  • A fully worked AAuth draft-11 example with narratives and consistent example values throughout

docs.title: Walkthrough Viewer
docs.text:
pidl generate -f viewer -o aauth.html aauth_protocol
Area Shows Menu bar Protocol name, scenario selector, theme, Present Sequence card Scenario introduction, the diagram with shared steps as labeled bands, the active step's narrative, and Overview, back, Step n / total and forward controls Request and response cards Request line, Host, headers and body; status, headers and body. Signed headers are marked; a Tokens tab decodes each token and highlights the claims the receiver checks

Keys: → and ← step, Home and End jump, P presents on a 16:9 stage. The URL records the scenario and step. See the Walkthrough Viewer guide.

docs.title: Flow Examples
docs.text: A flow's example holds a request, a response and decoded tokens, with a source citation and a kind: draft (taken from the source, values aligned to the scenario) or derived (written from its normative text). See the specification.

docs.title: Walkthrough Data
docs.text: generate -f walkthrough-json writes the data the viewer renders: every scenario with fragments expanded, each step's example and narrative, and analyzer findings attached to the steps they concern. Use it to build other viewers.

docs.title: AAuth Example
docs.text: Every step of the five access modes and the agent token, person token and consent fragments has a narrative and an example. Values are shared throughout: one agent key whose thumbprint is the resource token's agent_jkt, one person, and one timeline within the draft's token lifetimes. The agent token step follows the web app pattern of the AAuth Bootstrap guidance.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • For files with scenarios, analyzer findings from flow rules now point at the written scenario flow instead of an index into the flattened protocol.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go install github.com/grokify/pidl/cmd/pidl@v0.8.0

docs.title: PIDL v0.9.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-22

This release takes the walkthrough beyond one HTML file. The walkthrough is now a documented format that any page can show with one script tag from a CDN. Each request can be read as HTTP, as a curl command or as SDK code from tested source files, and each implementation of a protocol can keep its own code samples, so the protocol document stays independent of any of them. Steps can be narrated in several languages for audio and video, and the same examples drive a runnable Postman collection.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Embeddable viewer: @grokify/pidl-viewer shows any walkthrough from a CDN with one script tag
  • Walkthrough format: pidl-walkthrough/v1, with a JSON Schema and TypeScript types
  • Code samples and cURL: each request as HTTP, a generated curl command, or SDK code from tested source files; sample sets keep each implementation's code apart from the protocol
  • Postman collections: a runnable collection per protocol, with values chained between requests, checks on every response, and signed requests sent through a signing proxy
  • Narration: spoken text by language, scenario briefings and pronunciations
  • A worked OAuth 2.0 example that exercises all of it

docs.title: Embeddable Viewer
docs.text:
<div id="walkthrough"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"
        data-pidl-target="#walkthrough"
        data-pidl-src="api.walkthrough.json"></script>

The script shows a walkthrough from inline JSON (data-pidl-data), a URL (data-pidl-src) or the page's ?src= parameter, so one page can show any walkthrough. PidlViewer.mount(element, {src | data}) does the same from JavaScript.

  • The viewer renders inside a shadow root: the page's styles do not change it, and its styles do not leak into the page.
  • Several viewers can share a page. Each takes the step keys only while it has focus.
  • ?src= loads only https: URLs or the page's own origin, and fetches without cookies.

pidl generate -f viewer still writes one self-contained HTML file for offline use. See Embedding the Viewer.

docs.title: Walkthrough Format
docs.text:
pidl generate -f walkthrough-json writes pidl-walkthrough/v1, the processed form viewers read: every scenario with fragments expanded, each step's example, generated curl command, samples and narration, and analyzer findings. The format is now documented and versioned:

  • schema/walkthrough.schema.json is generated from the Go types and embedded as schema.WalkthroughSchemaJSON, with a test that it is current and that every built-in example validates.
  • The viewer's TypeScript types are generated from the schema, and ship in the npm package.
  • A reader accepts any v1 walkthrough, including one with fields it does not know, and refuses another major version.

See the walkthrough format reference.

docs.title: Code Samples and cURL
docs.text:
Every example request now has an equivalent curl command. A signed request's command replays the example's signature headers and says so.

Steps can also show code samples, ideally taken from a region between pidl:begin and pidl:end markers in a tested file, at a tag or commit. In the viewer, each request and response has a tab for HTTP, cURL and every sample language. A step where nothing goes over HTTP, such as a person approving in a browser, can show code alone.

Sample sets keep samples out of the protocol document. An implementation keeps a set (pidl-samples/v1) beside its tested code, attaching each sample to a step by its address, and generation joins any number of sets:

pidl samples resolve --repo-dir . sdk-go.pidl-samples.json            # record the code and its hash in the set
pidl samples check --repo-dir . --protocol api.json sdk-go.pidl-samples.json   # in the SDK's CI
pidl generate -f viewer --samples sdk-go.pidl-samples.json --samples sdk-ts.pidl-samples.json -o api.html api.json

An address that names no step is an error, so a set cannot fall silently behind the protocol. Samples can also be written inline on a step's example, with a lock file beside the document. The set format has its own schema, schema/samples.schema.json. See Code Samples and cURL.

docs.title: Postman Collections
docs.text:
pidl generate -f postman --signer proxy -o api.postman_collection.json oauth2_api_access

A folder for each scenario holds a request for each step the client role sends. Values a response delivers are passed to the requests that reuse them, including string parameters of headers, such as the scope of a WWW-Authenticate challenge. Each response is checked against its example, and deferred responses are polled.

  • --signer proxy sends requests with HTTP message signatures through a signing proxy, which creates the signature; Signature-Key tells it the scheme and, for the jwt scheme, the chained token to present. Unsigned requests are sent directly.
  • --mock saves the example responses for a Postman mock server.
  • -f postman-environment writes an environment for a named target, with per-scenario overrides.

See Postman Collections.

docs.title: Narration
docs.text: Scenarios and steps can carry narration keyed by BCP 47 language, with the protocol's source language as the fallback. Scenarios can carry a briefing, steps can override their narration for the HTTP, cURL or code view, and pronunciations tell text-to-speech tools how to say terms. The walkthrough carries all of it for audio and video tools; the viewer does not play narration yet. See Narration.

docs.title: Scenario Structure
docs.text:
• Groups order scenarios into sections.
  • Variants pair alternative forms of one journey and follow their base.
  • Step IDs name steps, as <include>.<id> inside fragments, so links such as #client-credentials/call.api-request keep working when steps are added, and sample sets can address them.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text: oauth2_api_access walks through calling an API with OAuth 2.0, with messages drawn from the RFCs: the authorization code grant with PKCE, client credentials, a variant after a Bearer scope challenge, an asynchronous export answered 202 and polled, and a request signed with HTTP Message Signatures and Content-Digest. It has shared fragments, decoded JWT access tokens, step IDs, narration, a briefing and pronunciations, and it is the example the guides use.

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
• Protocol.WithSampleSet, ParseSampleSet and CheckoutSourceReader for sample sets.
  • ResolveOptions.FS resolves the documents that extends and imports name from an fs.FS.
  • Built-in examples apply their sample lock and resolve their extends when loaded.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • The aauth_protocol and aauth_petstore examples, with the AAuth example's Go sample lock. pidl's built-in examples describe no single protocol in depth and carry no implementation's code; protocol documents and their walkthroughs belong with the protocol, and code samples with each implementation.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Sample source paths are checked the same way on every platform. The check used filepath.IsAbs, which does not treat /etc/passwd as absolute on Windows, so a test failed there. pidl now uses ValidateSlashPath from oscompat v0.8.0, its first dependency, which depends only on the standard library.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• New guides: Code Samples and cURL, Narration, Postman Collections and Embedding the Viewer.
  • New walkthrough format reference, and sample sets in the specification.
  • The CLI reference covers the samples command, the Postman formats and the new options.

docs.text:
go install github.com/grokify/pidl/cmd/pidl@v0.9.0

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@grokify/pidl-viewer@0.9.0/dist-lib/pidl-viewer.js"></script>

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
The following are explicitly out of scope for PIDL:

  • HTTP/transport-level details - Use OpenAPI for that
  • Message schema definitions - Use JSON Schema or protobuf
  • Code generation for implementation - PIDL describes, not implements
  • Full formal verification - Use TLA+ for rigorous proofs

docs.title: Process Spec Profile - Product Requirements Document
docs.text: Feature: Process Spec Profile for PIDL Version: 1.0 Status: Draft Author: Generated from IDEATION_PROCESSSPEC.md analysis

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Extend PIDL to support Process Spec - a profile for describing workflow and process semantics. This enables PIDL to model not just protocol choreography but also data pipelines, AI/LLM workflows, and multi-step processes with rich node semantics.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Current PIDL excels at describing "who talks to whom, in what order" for protocols like OAuth and MCP. However, modern systems require describing:

  • Data pipelines - ETL/ELT with deterministic transformations
  • AI/LLM workflows - Non-deterministic processing with model policies
  • Multi-step processes - VisionSpec-style document generation flows
  • Hybrid processes - Mixing deterministic validation with LLM generation

Users currently must use separate tools (BPMN, custom YAML) to describe these workflows, losing the benefits of PIDL's diagram generation, validation, and analysis capabilities.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. G1: Enable PIDL to describe process/workflow semantics without breaking existing protocol support
  2. G2: Support differentiation between deterministic and non-deterministic (LLM) processing steps
  3. G3: Generate the same diagram outputs (PlantUML, Mermaid, D2, SVG) from process specs
  4. G4: Maintain backward compatibility with existing PIDL documents
  5. G5: Enable security analysis and simulation for process flows

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Full BPMN compatibility (use dedicated BPMN tools for that)
  • Code generation for workflow execution engines
  • Runtime execution of processes (simulation only)
  • Process mining or discovery from logs

docs.title: US1: AI Workflow Designer
docs.text:
As an AI systems architect, I want to describe an LLM-powered document generation pipeline so that I can visualize the flow, identify non-deterministic steps, and generate documentation.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Can define nodes with stepType: llm vs stepType: deterministic
  • Can specify inputs (files, objects, APIs) and outputs
  • Generated diagrams show processing type visually
  • Can run simulation to trace execution

docs.title: US2: Data Pipeline Engineer
docs.text:
As a data engineer, I want to describe ETL pipelines in PIDL so that I can use the same tooling for both API protocols and data flows.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Can define source, transform, and sink nodes
  • Can specify data lineage through flows
  • Can annotate PII/sensitive data handling
  • DOT/D2 output shows data flow direction

docs.title: US3: VisionSpec User
docs.text:
As a VisionSpec user, I want to describe the MRD → PRD → TRD → Execution Spec pipeline so that I can visualize and validate the document generation process.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Can model the full VisionSpec document flow
  • Can distinguish between deterministic parsing and LLM generation
  • Can specify quality gates between steps
  • Can generate both sequence and data flow diagrams

docs.title: US4: Security Analyst
docs.text:
As a security analyst, I want to identify which process steps involve non-deterministic LLM processing so that I can focus review on those areas.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Security analysis flags LLM steps for review
  • Can annotate guardrails and validation requirements
  • Trust boundary analysis works with process nodes

docs.title: FR1: Profile Identification
docs.text:
• PIDL documents MUST support a kind field to identify the profile
  • Valid values: protocol (default), process
  • Existing documents without kind are treated as protocol

docs.title: FR2: Process Node Semantics
docs.text:
Process entities MUST support additional fields:

Field Type Description step_type enum deterministic, llm, human, external, tool inputs array Input specifications outputs array Output specifications processing object Processing configuration failure_modes array Possible failure scenarios retry_strategy object Retry configuration

docs.title: FR3: Input/Output Specifications
docs.text:
Inputs and outputs MUST specify:

Field Type Description kind enum file, object, api, database, queue, stream name string Identifier for the input/output schema string Optional reference to JSON Schema required bool Whether this input is required

docs.title: FR4: Processing Configuration
docs.text:
The processing object MUST support:

Field Type Description engine string Processing engine identifier determinism enum deterministic, non_deterministic model_policy string For LLM steps, the model selection policy timeout duration Maximum processing time idempotent bool Whether the step is idempotent

docs.title: FR5: Diagram Generation
docs.text:
• Sequence diagrams MUST render process flows like protocol flows
  • Data flow diagrams MUST show inputs/outputs on edges
  • Process nodes SHOULD be visually distinguished by step_type
  • SVG output SHOULD use different colors/icons for deterministic vs LLM

docs.title: FR6: Validation
docs.text:
• Process specs MUST validate that all inputs are produced by prior steps or defined as external
  • Circular dependencies MUST be detected and rejected
  • Required inputs MUST have producing flows

docs.title: FR7: Simulation
docs.text:
• Simulator MUST track input/output availability
  • Simulator MUST flag steps that cannot execute due to missing inputs
  • Trace output MUST include step type and processing metadata

docs.title: NFR1: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
• Existing PIDL documents MUST parse and render without modification
  • Default kind is protocol for documents without explicit kind

docs.title: NFR2: Schema Evolution
docs.text:
• New fields MUST be optional with sensible defaults
  • Schema version MUST be incremented

docs.title: NFR3: Performance
docs.text:
• Validation and rendering performance MUST not regress for protocol specs
  • Process spec validation MAY have additional O(n) passes for dependency analysis

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text: Metric Target Existing tests pass 100% New process spec examples 3+ (VisionSpec, ETL, LLM pipeline) Diagram formats supporting process All existing formats Documentation coverage Full spec + examples

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• PIDL v0.4.0 (current)
  • No external dependencies required

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation Schema complexity explosion Medium High Start minimal, add fields incrementally Breaking existing users Low High Strict backward compatibility, default kind Diagram rendering confusion Medium Medium Clear visual distinction for step types

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: See ROADMAP.md for phased delivery plan.

docs.title: Process Spec Profile - Technical Requirements Document
docs.text: Feature: Process Spec Profile for PIDL Version: 1.0 Status: Draft

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document describes the technical design for adding Process Spec profile support to PIDL. The design extends existing types and renderers while maintaining full backward compatibility.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Profile as extension - Process Spec adds fields to existing types, not parallel hierarchies
  2. Graceful degradation - Process-specific fields are ignored by protocol-focused tooling
  3. Shared rendering - Same renderer interface, enhanced output for process semantics
  4. Incremental adoption - Users can add process fields to existing protocol specs

docs.text:

│  parse.go          │ JSON parsing (unchanged)               │

docs.title: Protocol Kind Extension
docs.text:
Add to types.go:

// ProtocolKind identifies the PIDL profile type.
type ProtocolKind string

const (
    // ProtocolKindProtocol is the default for protocol choreography.
    ProtocolKindProtocol ProtocolKind = "protocol"
    // ProtocolKindProcess is for workflow/process specifications.
    ProtocolKindProcess ProtocolKind = "process"
)

Extend ProtocolMeta:

type ProtocolMeta struct {
    // ... existing fields ...

    // Kind identifies the PIDL profile type.
    Kind ProtocolKind `json:"kind,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: Process Step Types
docs.text:
// StepType classifies the processing nature of a step.
type StepType string

const (
    // StepTypeDeterministic is for repeatable, predictable processing.
    StepTypeDeterministic StepType = "deterministic"
    // StepTypeLLM is for LLM/AI-powered non-deterministic processing.
    StepTypeLLM StepType = "llm"
    // StepTypeHuman is for human-in-the-loop steps.
    StepTypeHuman StepType = "human"
    // StepTypeExternal is for external API/service calls.
    StepTypeExternal StepType = "external"
    // StepTypeTool is for tool invocations (MCP-style).
    StepTypeTool StepType = "tool"
)

docs.title: Entity Extensions for Process
docs.text:
Extend Entity with optional process fields:

type Entity struct {
    // ... existing fields ...

    // StepType classifies the processing nature (process profile).
    StepType StepType `json:"step_type,omitempty"`

    // Inputs defines input specifications (process profile).
    Inputs []DataPort `json:"inputs,omitempty"`

    // Outputs defines output specifications (process profile).
    Outputs []DataPort `json:"outputs,omitempty"`

    // Processing configures step execution (process profile).
    Processing *ProcessingConfig `json:"processing,omitempty"`

    // FailureModes lists possible failure scenarios (process profile).
    FailureModes []FailureMode `json:"failure_modes,omitempty"`

    // RetryStrategy configures retry behavior (process profile).
    RetryStrategy *RetryStrategy `json:"retry_strategy,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: Data Port (Input/Output)
docs.text:
// DataPort represents an input or output of a process step.
type DataPort struct {
    // Kind classifies the data type.
    Kind DataPortKind `json:"kind"`

    // Name is the identifier for this port.
    Name string `json:"name"`

    // Description provides additional context.
    Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`

    // Schema is an optional reference to a JSON Schema.
    Schema string `json:"schema,omitempty"`

    // Required indicates if this input must be provided.
    Required bool `json:"required,omitempty"`

    // Sensitive marks data as containing PII or secrets.
    Sensitive bool `json:"sensitive,omitempty"`
}

// DataPortKind classifies the type of data port.
type DataPortKind string

const (
    DataPortKindFile     DataPortKind = "file"
    DataPortKindObject   DataPortKind = "object"
    DataPortKindAPI      DataPortKind = "api"
    DataPortKindDatabase DataPortKind = "database"
    DataPortKindQueue    DataPortKind = "queue"
    DataPortKindStream   DataPortKind = "stream"
)

docs.title: Processing Configuration
docs.text:
// ProcessingConfig describes how a step processes its inputs.
type ProcessingConfig struct {
    // Engine identifies the processing engine.
    Engine string `json:"engine,omitempty"`

    // Determinism indicates processing predictability.
    Determinism Determinism `json:"determinism,omitempty"`

    // ModelPolicy specifies model selection for LLM steps.
    ModelPolicy string `json:"model_policy,omitempty"`

    // Timeout is the maximum processing duration.
    Timeout string `json:"timeout,omitempty"`

    // Idempotent indicates if repeated execution is safe.
    Idempotent bool `json:"idempotent,omitempty"`

    // Cacheable indicates if outputs can be cached.
    Cacheable bool `json:"cacheable,omitempty"`

    // CacheTTL is the cache time-to-live if cacheable.
    CacheTTL string `json:"cache_ttl,omitempty"`
}

// Determinism classifies processing predictability.
type Determinism string

const (
    DeterminismDeterministic    Determinism = "deterministic"
    DeterminismNonDeterministic Determinism = "non_deterministic"
)

docs.text:
// FailureMode describes a possible failure scenario.
type FailureMode struct {
    // ID is the unique identifier for this failure mode.
    ID string `json:"id"`

    // Name is the human-readable name.
    Name string `json:"name"`

    // Description explains the failure scenario.
    Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`

    // Severity indicates the impact level.
    Severity string `json:"severity,omitempty"`

    // Recovery describes how to handle this failure.
    Recovery string `json:"recovery,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text:
// RetryStrategy configures retry behavior for a step.
type RetryStrategy struct {
    // MaxAttempts is the maximum number of retry attempts.
    MaxAttempts int `json:"max_attempts,omitempty"`

    // InitialDelay is the delay before the first retry.
    InitialDelay string `json:"initial_delay,omitempty"`

    // MaxDelay is the maximum delay between retries.
    MaxDelay string `json:"max_delay,omitempty"`

    // BackoffMultiplier increases delay between retries.
    BackoffMultiplier float64 `json:"backoff_multiplier,omitempty"`

    // RetryOn lists failure mode IDs that trigger retry.
    RetryOn []string `json:"retry_on,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: New Validation Rules
docs.text:
Add validate_process.go:

// ValidateProcess performs process-specific validation.
func (p *Protocol) ValidateProcess() ValidationErrors {
    var errs ValidationErrors

    if p.ProtocolMeta.Kind != ProtocolKindProcess {
        return errs // Skip for non-process specs
    }

    // VP001: Validate input/output connectivity
    errs = append(errs, p.validateDataFlow()...)

    // VP002: Detect circular dependencies
    errs = append(errs, p.validateNoCycles()...)

    // VP003: Required inputs must have producers
    errs = append(errs, p.validateRequiredInputs()...)

    // VP004: StepType consistency
    errs = append(errs, p.validateStepTypes()...)

    return errs
}

docs.title: Validation Error Codes
docs.text: Code Description VP001 Disconnected data port (input has no producer, output has no consumer) VP002 Circular dependency detected in data flow VP003 Required input has no producing flow VP004 Invalid step type for entity type combination VP005 LLM step missing model_policy VP006 Retry strategy references unknown failure mode

docs.title: New Security Rules
docs.text:
Add to analyze/rules.go:

Rule Severity Description SEC011 Medium LLM step without output validation SEC012 High Sensitive data flows to LLM step SEC013 Medium Non-deterministic step in critical path SEC014 Low Missing failure mode for external step SEC015 Medium Human step without approval timeout

docs.title: Rule Implementation
docs.text:
// SEC011: LLM step without output validation
func checkLLMOutputValidation(p *Protocol) []SecurityRisk {
    var risks []SecurityRisk
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        if e.StepType == StepTypeLLM {
            if !hasDownstreamValidation(p, e.ID) {
                risks = append(risks, SecurityRisk{
                    Rule:     "SEC011",
                    Severity: SeverityMedium,
                    Entity:   e.ID,
                    Message:  "LLM step output not validated by downstream deterministic step",
                })
            }
        }
    }
    return risks
}

Extend ExecutionState:

type ExecutionState struct {

docs.title: Execution Logic
docs.text:
func (e *Executor) canExecuteStep(entity *Entity) bool {
    if entity.StepType == "" {
        return true // Not a process step, use default logic
    }

    for _, input := range entity.Inputs {
        if input.Required {
            key := fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s", entity.ID, input.Name)
            if !e.state.AvailableData[key] {
                return false
            }
        }
    }
    return true
}

docs.title: PLAN — Ordered roles and multiple scenarios per protocol
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text:
• The PRD and TRD are approved, including the naming decision ("scenario") and the ordering rule (array position only).
  • The current golden-file tests pass on main. They are the baseline for byte-for-byte compatibility.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Model and ordering
docs.text: Add the Scenario type, include steps, ordering helpers, validation and single-scenario projection. Write the "Ordering" section of the specification first, so that every later item follows the same rules. At the end of this phase, a file with scenarios parses, validates and projects. Legacy files behave as before.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Rendering and CLI
docs.text: Add --scenario, --all-scenarios with ordered file names, collapsed include rendering in every sequence format, and the scenarios command. At the end of this phase, every main scenario of a multi-scenario file can be rendered.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Overview outputs and verification semantics
docs.text: Add the scenario matrix, token table and outline outputs. Add the verification fields on tokens and flow security, and the analyzer rules that use them. At the end of this phase, a protocol's roles, tokens and scenarios can be documented in one consistent order.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Composition, diff, example, release
docs.text: Make extends, imports and diff scenario-aware. Add the AAuth example as the end-to-end test. Update the schema, specification, guide and changelog, and release v0.7.0 together with the pending D2, determinism and line-ending fixes.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Legacy output changes Golden files for existing examples gate every PR Include boxes render differently by format One golden file per format, plus visual review of the AAuth diagrams Index-based references break under expansion Re-base indices during projection; nested-include table tests The AAuth draft changes during the work Pin the example to draft -11 in its references; pidl diff covers later drafts

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text:
• Deck and guide generators that read outline-json, such as a Marp deck template.
  • A pidl migrate command that wraps a legacy flows file into a single scenario.
  • Splitting the legacy metadata.networks map into an ordered array in the next schema major version.

docs.title: PRD — Ordered roles and multiple scenarios per protocol
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A PIDL file describes one protocol as a list of entities and a single ordered list of flows. Real protocols are not one flow. AAuth, for example, has seven roles, five access modes and about eight shared sub-flows (agent bootstrap, discovery, interaction, deferred response, mission lifecycle, step-up, call chaining, revocation). Documenting it today means one file per flow, tied together with imports or extends. That leaves four gaps:

  1. No shared order. Each file decides its own entity order, and there is no order across flows. A slide deck, a guide and a set of diagrams generated from those files can each present roles and flows in a different sequence.
  2. No reuse inside a flow. A shared sub-flow such as "interaction" has to be copied into every flow that uses it, or left out.
  3. No checks across flows. Validation runs per file, so it cannot report a role that no flow uses or a token that is used before any flow issues it.
  4. No overview outputs. Nothing renders a roles × flows table or a token table for the whole protocol.

Flow.sequence adds confusion: it is documented as "explicit ordering" but no code sorts by it, so its value never affects the output.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• One PIDL file can hold a protocol's roles and an ordered list of named scenarios, each with its own ordered flows.
  • Array position is the only source of order, for roles, scenarios, phases and flows. Every output (diagram, table, outline) shows the same order.
  • A scenario can include another scenario as a reusable fragment, shown as a labeled box or expanded in place.
  • Validation and analysis work across all scenarios in a file.
  • New outputs give an overview of the whole protocol: a roles × scenarios matrix, a token table and an ordered outline that guides and presentations can be built from.
  • Existing files keep working without changes.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Generating slide decks or guides directly. PIDL emits ordered, structured outputs. Deck and guide tools consume them.
  • A "journey" concept tied to human users or UX. Scenarios cover flows with or without a person. A display name can say "journey" where an audience prefers it.
  • Message schemas or transport details. These stay out of scope as stated in the main roadmap.
  • Numeric ordering fields. Order comes from array position only.

docs.title: Users and Stakeholders
docs.text:
• Protocol reviewers who need one diagram per scenario, plus a token table that shows who issues and who checks each token.
  • Developer relations and educators who build presentations and guides and need roles and scenarios in the same order everywhere.
  • Spec authors who track how a draft changes between versions. pidl diff should report scenario-level changes.
  • Tool builders who use the Go library and need a stable API for one scenario at a time.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
1. Scenarios. A protocol file MAY contain a top-level scenarios array. Each scenario has an id, a name, an optional description, an optional participants list, an optional fragment flag and a flows array.
  2. Includes. An entry in a scenario's flows array MAY be an include step ({"include": "<scenario-id>"}) instead of a message.
  3. Ordering rule.
  4. The order of the entities array sets the order of roles everywhere.
  5. The order of the scenarios array sets the order of scenarios.
  6. The order of the phases array sets the order of phases.
  7. The order of flows within a scenario sets the order of messages.
  8. Participants follow entity order. A scenario's participants list selects roles. It never reorders them. A list that is out of order is a validation error.
  9. Default participants. When participants is omitted, a scenario's participants are the entities its flows and includes use, in entities order.
  10. Fragments. A scenario with "fragment": true can be included by other scenarios. Commands that render every scenario skip fragments unless asked to include them.
  11. Backward compatibility.
  12. A file with a top-level flows array and no scenarios behaves exactly as it does today.
  13. A file that has both a non-empty flows array and a scenarios array is invalid.
  14. Single-scenario projection. The library can turn one scenario into a single-flow Protocol, so every existing renderer, the executor and the debugger work on it unchanged.
  15. CLI selection. generate, simulate, debug and analyze accept --scenario <id>.
  16. Rendering every scenario. generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> writes one file per scenario. Each file name starts with a zero-padded position, such as 01-agent-identity.mmd, so sorting the files by name keeps scenario order.
  17. Collapsed includes. By default, a renderer draws an include as a labeled box over the fragment's participants. --expand inlines the fragment's flows instead.
  18. Overview outputs:
    • a roles × scenarios matrix
    • a token table: issuer, audience, binding, who checks it and the claims they rely on
    • an ordered outline (Markdown and JSON) listing roles, then scenarios with their steps
  19. Verification semantics.
    • TokenDefinition records who checks each token and which claims they rely on.
    • FlowSecurity records who signs a request and which tokens the receiver checks.
  20. Checks across scenarios. The analyzer reports:
    • roles used by no scenario
    • tokens checked in a flow before any earlier step issued them
    • flows signed by someone other than the sender, unless annotated
    • token checkers that are not participants of the scenario
  21. Composition.
    • extends and imports merge scenarios by id, base scenarios first.
    • exclude_scenarios removes scenarios from the base.
  22. Diff. pidl diff matches scenarios by id and reports scenarios that were added or removed, changed flows, and changes in the order of roles or scenarios.
  23. Flow.sequence deprecation. The field is documented as display only, and no code may sort by it.
  24. Example. The built-in examples include AAuth, with seven roles, five main scenarios and its shared fragments.

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• Deterministic output. The same input always produces identical output. No output order may depend on Go map iteration.
  • No change for existing files. For every existing example, generate output stays byte-for-byte the same.
  • Library first. All behavior lives in the pidl and render packages. The CLI only parses flags and calls them.
  • The JSON Schema in schema/pidl.schema.json describes the new fields and validates every example.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The AAuth example validates and renders five main scenario diagrams in Mermaid, PlantUML and D2, with roles in the same column order.
  • --all-scenarios output and the outline list scenarios in the same order as the file.
  • The golden-file tests for existing examples pass unchanged.
  • A four-party AAuth scenario annotated with signed_by makes the analyzer report that the PS, not the agent, signs the request to the AS.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Flow index references. exclude_flows and ParallelBranch.flow_refs use indices into the top-level flows array. Inside scenarios they need a scenario scope. Mitigation: index within the scenario, and reject index references that don't say which scenario they mean.
  • Collapsed include rendering differs by format. Mermaid has no ref fragment. Mitigation: use rect plus a note in Mermaid, ref over in PlantUML and a group in D2, and test each with golden files.
  • Schema growth. New optional fields make the format larger. Mitigation: all are optional, and the scenario fields are grouped together in the specification.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• "Scenario" rather than "journey". "Journey" usually means a human user's path through a product. Many protocol scenarios have no person in them (for example agent-to-resource identity). "Scenario" is the common term in specs and testing, and it fits PIDL's simulator ("run scenario four-party"). Display names may still say "journey".
  • Array position is the only order. A second mechanism (numeric order or sequence fields) lets outputs drift apart.
  • Fragments are scenarios. Shared sub-flows use the same type, so the ordering and validation rules need no special cases.
  • Collapsed by default. Presentations and overview diagrams read better with a sub-flow drawn as one labeled box. --expand serves detailed review.

docs.title: ROADMAP — Ordered roles and multiple scenarios per protocol
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

One PIDL file holds a protocol's ordered roles and an ordered list of scenarios. Array position is the only source of order, so diagrams, guides and presentations generated from the file agree. Commits implementing an item carry Refs: RMI-PIDL-<NNN>.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Composition, Diff, Example and Release
