docs.title: TRD — Ordered roles and multiple scenarios per protocol
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• Protocol (types.go) has Entities []Entity, Phases []Phase and Flows []Flow. A file describes exactly one flow.
  • Sequence renderers (render/mermaid.go, render/plantuml.go, render/d2.go) declare participants by iterating p.Entities, so column order already follows the array. Each renderer declares every entity, including ones the flow never uses.
  • Flow.Sequence is documented as "explicit ordering". The only place it is read is a non-negative check (validate_flow.go). Nothing sorts by it.
  • ProtocolMetadata.Networks is a map[string]*NetworkConfig. Its order is undefined unless network_layout.order is set.
  • ProtocolExtends.ExcludeFlows and ParallelBranch.FlowRefs are integer indices into Protocol.Flows.
  • Executor and Debugger index into Protocol.Flows directly.
  • render/markdown_matrix.go builds an entities × protocol-roles table and sorts the protocol columns alphabetically.
  • ValidationError has no severity, so every reported problem is an error.

docs.title: 1. Types
docs.text:
// Scenario is a named, ordered sequence of flows within a protocol.
type Scenario struct {
    ID           string   `json:"id"`
    Name         string   `json:"name"`
    Description  string   `json:"description,omitempty"`
    Participants []string `json:"participants,omitempty"` // subset of entity IDs, in entity order
    Fragment     bool     `json:"fragment,omitempty"`     // reusable via include; skipped by --all-scenarios
    Flows        []Flow   `json:"flows"`
}

type Protocol struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    Flows     []Flow     `json:"flows,omitempty"`     // was required; now optional when Scenarios is set
    Scenarios []Scenario `json:"scenarios,omitempty"`
}

type Flow struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    // Include references a scenario whose flows are inserted at this
    // point. When set, From, To and Action must be empty.
    Include string `json:"include,omitempty"`
    // Sequence is a display-only step number. It never affects order.
    // Deprecated: order is the position in the flows array.
    Sequence int `json:"sequence,omitempty"`
}

Verification semantics:

type TokenDefinition struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    VerifiedBy []string     `json:"verified_by,omitempty"` // entity IDs, in entity order
    Claims     []TokenClaim `json:"claims,omitempty"`      // ordered
}

type TokenClaim struct {
    Name        string   `json:"name"`
    CheckedBy   []string `json:"checked_by,omitempty"`
    Description string   `json:"description,omitempty"`
}

type FlowSecurity struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    SignedBy string   `json:"signed_by,omitempty"` // entity ID; defaults to Flow.From
    Issues   []string `json:"issues,omitempty"`    // token IDs carried in the response
    Verifies []string `json:"verifies,omitempty"`  // token IDs the receiver checks
}

type ProtocolExtends struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    ExcludeScenarios []string `json:"exclude_scenarios,omitempty"`
}

Issues and Verifies give the analyzer the data it needs for the "used before issued" check without a full simulation.

docs.title: 2. Ordering rules
docs.text:
These rules are normative in docs/SPECIFICATION.md:

  1. Role order is the order of entities.
  2. Scenario order is the order of scenarios.
  3. Phase order is the order of phases.
  4. Message order within a scenario is the order of its flows. An include expands in place.
  5. Every list derived from these arrays keeps their order. Examples are participants, token checkers, matrix rows and columns, outline entries and generated file names.
  6. Collections keyed by name must be arrays of objects with an id. metadata.networks stays a map for compatibility, but renderers order it by network_layout.order when set and otherwise by first appearance of its entities in entities. They never order it by map iteration.

Helpers in a new file order.go:

func (p *Protocol) EntityIndex(id string) int          // -1 if absent
func (p *Protocol) OrderEntities(ids []string) []string // stable sort by EntityIndex
func (p *Protocol) ScenarioIDs(includeFragments bool) []string

docs.title: 3. Validation (validate_scenario.go)
docs.text:
Added to Protocol.Validate():

  • flows must be non-empty when scenarios is empty, and empty when scenarios is non-empty.
  • Scenario ids are unique and match the existing ID pattern.
  • Every participants entry is an entity ID. The list has no duplicates and is in entity order. Out-of-order lists fail with a message that gives the expected order.
  • Each flow is either an include (only include, plus optional phase, note, condition) or a message (from, to, action). It cannot be both.
  • include targets exist and have fragment: true.
  • Includes form no cycle. The check is a depth-first search with the path in the error.
  • When participants is set, every flow's from and to and every included fragment's participants are in it.
  • FlowSecurity.SignedBy, TokenDefinition.VerifiedBy and TokenClaim.CheckedBy reference entity IDs. Issues/Verifies reference token IDs.
  • ParallelBranch.FlowRefs inside a scenario are indices into that scenario's flows.

The existing per-flow checks in validate_flow.go run on each scenario's flows. Errors carry the path, for example scenarios[2].flows[4].to.

docs.title: 4. Projection (scenario.go)
docs.text:
type ProjectOptions struct {
    Expand bool // inline included fragments; default renders them as include steps
}

// Scenario returns a single-flow Protocol for scenario id. Entities are
// filtered to the scenario's participants in entity order; phases are
// filtered to those referenced, in phase order; metadata is copied.
func (p *Protocol) Scenario(id string, opts ProjectOptions) (*Protocol, error)

// Legacy files: Scenario("", opts) returns p unchanged when Scenarios is empty.
  • With Expand, include steps are replaced recursively by the fragment's flows. Index-based references are re-based onto the expanded list.
  • Without Expand, include steps stay in Flows. Renderers that do not understand includes would break, so each sequence renderer gains an include case (section 5), and non-sequence renderers (DOT, network, infographic) always receive an expanded projection.
  • The projected protocol carries the scenario's id and name in ProtocolMeta (Name: "<protocol> — <scenario>") so titles render without renderer changes.

Executor and debugger run on a projection with Expand: true. Their index-based code is unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Rendering includes (collapsed)
docs.text:
The box spans the fragment's participants, from the first to the last in entity order.

Format Output PlantUML ref over a, b : <fragment name> Mermaid rect rgb(...) block containing Note over a,b: <fragment name> D2 sequence a group labeled with the fragment name, spanning the participants SVG a rounded rectangle across the participant lifelines, labeled

Golden files in render/testdata cover each format.

docs.title: 6. CLI (cmd/pidl)
docs.text:
• generate, simulate, debug and analyze take --scenario <id>. On a file with scenarios, omitting it is an error that lists the available IDs in order, except for analyze, which runs on all.
  • generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> writes NN-<scenario-id>.<ext>. NN is the 1-based position among non-fragment scenarios, zero-padded to at least two digits (wider when there are 100 or more scenarios). --include-fragments adds fragments after the main scenarios, with continued numbering.
  • --expand on generate inlines fragments.
  • New formats on generate:
  • scenario-matrix (Markdown) — rows are entities in order, columns are scenarios in order, cells mark participation.
  • token-table (Markdown) — rows are tokens in array order, with issuer, audience, binding, verified by and claims.
  • outline (Markdown) and outline-json — protocol, then roles in order with descriptions, then scenarios in order with each step's label (includes shown by fragment name). This is the input for deck and guide tooling.
  • pidl scenarios <file> lists scenarios in order, with the participant count, flow count and fragment flag. -f json gives JSON output.

docs.title: 7. Analyzer (analyze)
docs.text:
New rules, each with an ID, a severity and an explanation:

Rule Reports SEC017 Unused role an entity that no flow uses SEC018 Token checked before issued a flow verifies a token that no earlier step of the expanded scenario issues; tokens no flow issues are treated as external and skipped SEC019 Signer differs from sender or token holder signed_by differs from from, or a request presents a token that an earlier step delivered to someone other than the signer (the AAuth four-party agent_jkt case); skipped when the flow has a security annotation SEC020 Token verifier mismatch a flow's receiver checks a token whose verified_by does not list it SEC021 Unused fragment a fragment no scenario includes

Rules carry a scope. Flow rules (the existing SEC001 to SEC016) check Protocol.Flatten() for a document with scenarios; document rules receive the protocol as written and report scenario paths such as scenarios[1].flows[0] (exchange).

docs.title: 8. Composition (resolve.go)
docs.text:
• mergeBase: base scenarios come first. A derived scenario with the same id replaces the base one in its base position, so an override never reorders scenarios. New derived scenarios follow.
  • ExcludeScenarios runs before the merge. ExcludeEntities also drops scenario flows that reference an excluded entity and removes it from participants. ExcludePhases also clears phase references in scenario flows.
  • mergeImport: ProtocolImport.Scenarios []string selects scenarios to import. Fragments they include come with them, in the imported document's order. The alias prefix applies to scenario IDs, include targets, entity references, participants and phases.
  • Mixing documents with and without scenarios: when composition leaves both top-level flows and scenarios, the flows become the first scenario, with the resolved protocol's ID and name (plus a -flows suffix if that ID is taken).
  • The JSON Schema does not yet describe extends or imports; that gap predates this initiative.

docs.title: 9. Diff (compare.go)
docs.text:
• Scenarios are matched by id. The diff reports added, removed and renamed scenarios (same id, new name), as well as changed flows within each matched scenario, using the existing flow diff.
  • Order changes are reported separately for entities and scenarios ("moved from position 3 to 1").

docs.title: 10. Schema and specification
docs.text:
• schema/pidl.schema.json:
  • The top-level required drops flows.
  • It gains a oneOf requiring either a non-empty flows or a non-empty scenarios.
  • It gains the scenario and tokenClaim definitions, plus the new fields on flow, flowSecurity, tokenDefinition and extends.
  • docs/SPECIFICATION.md gets a "Scenarios" section and an "Ordering" section with the rules from section 2.

docs.title: Sequencing Constraints
docs.text:
• Types and validation come before projection, and projection before any renderer or CLI change.
  • Rendering includes depends on projection without expansion.
  • The analyzer rules depend on the verification fields.
  • The AAuth example depends on includes, verification fields and rendering. It serves as the end-to-end test.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Byte-for-byte compatibility. Changing a renderer for includes could alter output for legacy files. Mitigation: the existing golden files must pass unchanged, and include rendering only runs when a flow has Include set.
  • Unused-participant declarations. Projection drops entities a scenario does not use. Legacy files are not projected, so their output is unchanged.
  • Index re-basing on expansion. Errors here would misreport validation paths. Mitigation: table tests covering nested includes with parallel branches.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Unit tests:
  • ordering helpers
  • each validation rule, both pass and fail cases
  • projection with and without expansion, including nested fragments
  • cycle detection
  • Golden files: each sequence format for a collapsed include, an expanded include and the AAuth main scenarios.
  • CLI table tests: --scenario, --all-scenarios file naming and ordering, scenarios listing, and errors.
  • Determinism: render every format twice and compare the outputs. Also shuffle map-backed metadata by re-encoding the input and confirm the output is unchanged.
  • Schema: every file in examples/ validates against the updated schema.

docs.title: PRD — Protocol walkthrough viewer and AAuth examples
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-002 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
PIDL v0.7.0 can describe a protocol's roles and scenarios and render each scenario as a static sequence diagram. Static diagrams are a poor way to learn a protocol like AAuth:

  1. No step-by-step view. A five-party diagram with a dozen messages shows everything at once. A presenter cannot walk an audience through it one message at a time, and a reader cannot tell which roles take part in a given step.
  2. No message content. A diagram shows that the agent sends a resource token to the PS, but not what that request looks like: the signature headers, the body, or the claims inside the token. Readers have to cross-reference the specification.
  3. No connection between steps. A protocol's security depends on values that link steps: a resource token's agent_jkt must match the key that signs the request; presented_jti must match the token the agent presented. Static diagrams cannot show those links.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A generic viewer for any PIDL file: pick a scenario, step forward and backward through it, and see the active step highlighted on the sequence diagram (its two roles, its arrow and its label).
  • Example requests, responses and decoded tokens for each step, shown beside the diagram.
  • A 16:9 presentation layout that works full screen in a talk and in a browser tab.
  • One self-contained HTML file per protocol, with no server, so a walkthrough can be shared by sending a file.
  • A fully worked AAuth draft-11 example: every step of the five access modes and their fragments with requests, responses and tokens taken from or derived from the draft, using consistent values across steps.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Message schemas or protocol conformance checking. Examples are illustrative.
  • Editing PIDL in the viewer.
  • Live protocol execution against real servers.
  • Replacing the static diagram formats; the viewer is an additional output.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Presenters explaining a protocol in a talk or meeting.
  • Readers learning a protocol from its PIDL description.
  • Spec reviewers checking that the values each step relies on line up end to end.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
1. Flow examples. A flow MAY carry an example with a source (citation), a kind (draft: taken from the source with values aligned; derived: written from the source's normative text), an HTTP request and/or response (method or status, URL, ordered headers, body), and decoded tokens (header and payload) keyed to token definitions.
  2. Validation. kind is draft or derived; source is required; header names are non-empty; token references resolve to token definitions.
  3. Walkthrough model. The library produces a walkthrough document: protocol, roles in entities order, and for each scenario in output order its fully expanded steps. Each step carries its position, from and to roles, label, response flag, the fragments it sits inside, note, example, and analyzer findings located at that flow.
  4. Walkthrough output. generate -f walkthrough-json writes the walkthrough model.
  5. Viewer layout. A top bar with the protocol name and a scenario selector; a sequence diagram on the left; the request on the upper right; the response on the lower right; step controls.
  6. Stepping. Next and previous buttons, arrow keys, and Home/End. The active step's arrow, label and two role headers are highlighted; earlier steps are dimmed; later steps are faint. The URL hash records the scenario and step.
  7. Fragments. Steps inside an included fragment show the fragment's name; the diagram groups them visually.
  8. Tokens. Decoded token header and payload are shown in readable form; claims a step's receiver checks are highlighted.
  9. Findings and notes. A step's notes and analyzer findings appear as callouts.
  10. Example provenance. Each example shows its source and a draft or derived badge.
  11. Single-file output. generate -f viewer writes one HTML file containing the viewer and the walkthrough data.
  12. AAuth examples. The aauth_protocol example gains examples for every HTTP step of all five scenarios and three fragments, with one consistent set of identifiers, keys and token values.

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• The viewer renders the AAuth walkthrough in under a second on a laptop and works offline.
  • The viewer's built HTML is reproducible from source with one documented command.
  • Go code remains library-first; the viewer contains presentation logic only.
  • Existing output formats are unchanged.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• pidl generate -f viewer aauth_protocol -o aauth.html produces a file that opens in a browser and steps through all five AAuth scenarios.
  • In the federated scenario, stepping to the PS-to-AS request shows the request signed with the PS's key and the resource token whose agent_jkt names the agent's key, with the SEC019 finding as a callout.
  • Every AAuth example cites a draft-11 section.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Examples live in the PIDL file as an optional per-flow field, so they travel with the protocol.
  • Provenance is explicit. draft examples come from the draft with values aligned to the scenario; derived examples are written from normative text. The viewer shows which.
  • Go computes, the viewer renders. Include expansion, ordering and findings come from the Go library through the walkthrough model, so the viewer does not reimplement PIDL semantics.
  • Self-contained HTML. The viewer is built into a single file and embedded in the Go binary.
  • Ships as v0.8.0.

docs.title: TRD — Protocol walkthrough viewer and AAuth examples
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-002 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• Flow has no message content. Protocol.Outline() returns ordered roles and scenarios with numbered steps, but keeps include steps collapsed.
  • Protocol.Scenario(id, ProjectOptions{Expand: true}) expands includes but drops which fragment a step came from.
  • Analyzer risks carry a Location string such as scenarios[4].flows[6] (federated-authorization).
  • The repo has TypeScript only in integrations/; there is no web app.

docs.title: 1. Flow examples (types.go)
docs.text:
type FlowExample struct {
    Source   string            `json:"source"`             // e.g. "draft-11 §7.2.1"
    Kind     ExampleKind       `json:"kind"`               // "draft" | "derived"
    Request  *ExampleRequest   `json:"request,omitempty"`
    Response *ExampleResponse  `json:"response,omitempty"`
    Tokens   []ExampleToken    `json:"tokens,omitempty"`
    Note     string            `json:"note,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleRequest struct {
    Method  string          `json:"method"`
    URL     string          `json:"url"`
    Headers []ExampleHeader `json:"headers,omitempty"`
    Body    json.RawMessage `json:"body,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleResponse struct {
    Status  int             `json:"status"`
    Headers []ExampleHeader `json:"headers,omitempty"`
    Body    json.RawMessage `json:"body,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleHeader struct {
    Name  string `json:"name"`
    Value string `json:"value"`
}
type ExampleToken struct {
    Token   string          `json:"token"`             // token definition ID
    Label   string          `json:"label,omitempty"`   // e.g. "in Signature-Key"
    Header  json.RawMessage `json:"header,omitempty"`
    Payload json.RawMessage `json:"payload,omitempty"`
}
// Flow gains: Example *FlowExample `json:"example,omitempty"`

Headers are an ordered array, not a map, so they render in the order written. Bodies, token headers and payloads are json.RawMessage, so key order survives a round trip through Go.

docs.title: 2. Walkthrough model (walkthrough.go)
docs.text:
type Walkthrough struct {
    ID, Name, Description string
    Roles     []OutlineRole
    Scenarios []WalkthroughScenario
    Tokens    []OutlineToken
}
type WalkthroughScenario struct {
    Position int; ID, Name, Description string; Fragment bool
    Participants []string
    Steps []WalkthroughStep
}
type WalkthroughStep struct {
    Number   int      // 1-based within the expanded scenario
    From, To string
    Label    string
    Response bool
    Phase    string
    Fragments []string   // fragment names, outermost first
    Note     string
    Example  *FlowExample
    Location string      // written location, e.g. "scenarios[1].flows[0] (consent)"
    Findings []WalkthroughFinding
}
type WalkthroughFinding struct { ID, Severity, Title, Description string }

func (p *Protocol) Walkthrough(findings func(*Protocol) []Finding) Walkthrough
  • Steps come from expanding includes in order, recording each enclosing fragment's name.
  • Location uses the same strings as the analyzer's document rules, so findings attach by location. The pidl package cannot import analyze, so the caller passes findings in; the CLI and renderer run the analyzer.
  • Include steps disappear in expansion; their fragment name appears in Fragments of the inlined steps.

docs.title: 3. Formats
docs.text:
• walkthrough-json: the walkthrough model as JSON, a whole-file format.
  • viewer: the built viewer HTML with the walkthrough JSON embedded in a <script type="application/json" id="pidl-walkthrough"> element, a whole-file format.

docs.title: 4. Viewer app (viewer/)
docs.text:
• Vite 8, React 19, TypeScript, vite-plugin-singlefile; Vitest for unit tests.
  • Data: reads the embedded #pidl-walkthrough element; in development, loads public/walkthrough.json.
  • Layout: a fixed 1600×900 stage scaled to fit the window (16:9). Top bar: protocol name, scenario selector, step counter and controls. Left (60%): SVG sequence diagram drawn by the app. Right (40%): request panel above, response panel below, each with tabs for HTTP and tokens.
  • Diagram: role headers in walkthrough role order, limited to the scenario's participants; one row per step; fragment groups drawn as shaded bands labeled with the fragment name; the active step's arrow, label and role headers highlighted, earlier steps dimmed, later steps faint. The diagram scrolls to keep the active step visible.
  • Stepping: buttons, Left/Right arrows, Home/End; URL hash #<scenario-id>/<step>.
  • Panels: method, URL and headers; JSON body pretty-printed; decoded tokens with claims named in the receiver's checked_by highlighted; provenance badge (draft or derived) with source; notes and findings as callouts.
  • Theme: light and dark via prefers-color-scheme.

docs.title: 5. Build and embedding
docs.text:
• npm run build in viewer/ writes render/viewer/viewer.html (committed), which render embeds with go:embed.
  • go generate ./render/... runs the build; CI checks that the committed file matches a fresh build.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Committed build artifact drift. Mitigation: a CI check rebuilds and diffs.
  • Example accuracy. Examples could misstate the draft. Mitigation: each cites a section; draft versus derived is explicit; consistent identifiers are listed once in the example file's description of values.
  • Large diagrams. Five-party scenarios with fifteen steps must stay legible at 16:9. Mitigation: the diagram scrolls and keeps the active step in view.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Go: validation table tests for examples; walkthrough expansion with nested fragments, locations and findings; golden files for walkthrough-json; viewer output contains the embedded data.
  • Viewer: Vitest unit tests for layout computation, step navigation and hash parsing.
  • Manual: open the AAuth viewer in a browser and step through every scenario; screenshots in the PR.

  4. Viewer: left navigation and variants, autoplay, token lifecycle, representation tabs and raw tokens; documentation and v0.9.0.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Scope creep into AAuth content AAuth content lives in INIT-PIDL-004 Samples drift from SDKs Hashes recorded at resolve; samples check in CI

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text: INIT-PIDL-004 (AAuth coverage) and INIT-PIDL-005 (narrated video) build on this.

docs.title: PRD — PIDL for developer content
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-003 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
PIDL v0.8.0 describes a protocol's scenarios and shows one illustrative HTTP exchange per step in a walkthrough viewer. Developer relations needs more from the same source:

  1. Navigation for many scenarios. A complete protocol has dozens of scenarios in sections (AAuth: signing, bootstrap, access modes, missions, advanced patterns, R3). A dropdown does not scale, and PIDL has no notion of sections.
  2. Variants. The same scenario often has an autonomous and a with-approval form, or a web and a mobile form. Today each is an unrelated scenario.
  3. Stable step identity. Samples, deep links and narration need to target a step. Flow action values repeat (AAuth federated access has two auth_token steps), and array positions shift when steps are added.
  4. Spoken narration. On-screen narratives contain identifiers such as agent_jkt and aa-auth+jwt that read badly aloud. Video needs a script written for the ear, plus pronunciations.
  5. More than HTTP. Developers want the same message as cURL and as SDK code (Go, TypeScript, Python, C# and others). SDK code pasted into documents goes stale as SDKs change.
  6. Trustworthy examples. Examples are hand-assembled. Nothing checks that a Content-Digest matches its body, that an encoded token matches its decoded form, or that examples follow a protocol's rules (AAuth draft-11 forbids EdDSA, for instance). An existing AAuth explorer shows how easily these drift: its digests do not match its bodies and its tokens use algorithms draft-11 forbids.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• PIDL stays the single, protocol-neutral source of truth for protocol walkthroughs; nothing in this initiative is AAuth-specific except an optional check profile.
  • Scenarios can be grouped into ordered sections and related as variants.
  • Steps have stable identifiers.
  • Each scenario and step can carry a spoken narration script, and a protocol can declare pronunciations.
  • A message can be shown as HTTP, as generated cURL, and as SDK code drawn from tested source files.
  • Examples are checked: generic HTTP and JWT consistency for every protocol, and protocol-specific rules through profiles.
  • The viewer gains grouped left navigation, variant toggles, autoplay, a token lifecycle panel, and representation tabs.
  • The viewer reaches feature parity with dedicated protocol explorers: header and claim help, signature bases, deferred-response timelines, protocol documents, value tracing, comparison tables, and reference pages, all defined generically in PIDL.
  • Steps can carry guided tours: ordered beats that focus a region of the page with narration, for live autoplay and for narrated video.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Text-to-speech and video production (INIT-PIDL-005).
  • AAuth content beyond what tests need (INIT-PIDL-004).
  • Generating SDK code from PIDL. Samples come from real SDKs.
  • Executing samples or examples against live servers.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Developer relations writing tutorials, presentations and videos from one source.
  • Application developers learning to call a protocol from their language.
  • Spec authors and reviewers who need examples they can trust.
  • SDK maintainers whose tested examples appear in walkthroughs.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
1. Groups. A document MAY declare an ordered groups array (id, name, description). A scenario MAY name its group. Group order, then scenario order within a group, sets navigation order.
  2. Variants. A scenario MAY declare variant_of (another scenario's ID) and variant_label (e.g. "With user approval"). The base scenario and its variants share a navigation entry with a toggle.
  3. Flow IDs. A flow MAY have an id, unique within its scenario and matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$. The viewer accepts #<scenario>/<flow-id> as well as #<scenario>/<n>.
  4. Narration. Scenarios and flows MAY carry narration: plain text written to be spoken, as an object keyed by BCP 47 language ({"en-US": "…", "fr-FR": "…", "zh-Hans": "…"}). The document's protocol.language (default en-US) is the source language and the fallback when a language is missing. Briefing narration and tour beats use the same language-keyed form. A document MAY declare pronunciations, a map from a term to its spoken form per language ({"AAuth": {"en-US": "ay auth"}}), the same shape videoascode reads, so video tooling can use it unchanged. When narration is absent, tools fall back to description.
  5. Briefing. A scenario MAY carry a briefing for the slides that introduce it: why (prose on why the scenario exists and what problem it solves), points (a short ordered list of key points), and narration (what is spoken over those slides). The scenario description stays a one-paragraph summary.
  6. Samples. A flow example and a scenario MAY carry samples: each has a language, an optional label and role, and either inline code or a source reference (repo, path, region). Region markers in source files (pidl:begin <name> and pidl:end <name> in a comment) delimit the code.
  7. Sample resolution. pidl samples resolve fetches referenced regions from local checkouts and records each sample's content hash; generation embeds resolved code so viewers stay self-contained; a check fails when a referenced region is missing.
  8. Generated cURL. For any example request, tools generate an equivalent cURL command. The viewer notes that cURL replays the example's signature headers and cannot create HTTP message signatures.
  9. Example checks (generic): Content-Digest matches the body it covers; encoded JWTs in headers and bodies decode to the decoded tokens shown; every component named in Signature-Input is present; created and token iat/exp values are consistent; decoded token claims respect exp > iat.
  10. Check profiles. Protocol-specific rules live in named profiles (first: aauth-draft-11) selected by the document (protocol.profiles) or on the command line.
  11. Walkthrough data carries groups, variants, flow IDs, narration, briefings, pronunciations, resolved samples, generated cURL and token lifecycle events.

  12. Viewer: grouped left navigation; variant toggle; play, pause and replay with speeds (0.5× to 3×) and per-step durations from narration length; a token lifecycle panel (issued, forwarded, presented, checked); a decoded/raw token toggle; representation tabs (HTTP, cURL, and each sample language) with the chosen language remembered.

  13. Glossary. A document MAY declare a glossary of headers, claims and terms (term, kind, category, description, optional reference). The viewer shows descriptions as help on headers and claims and badges terms by category (for example, protocol-defined headers).

  14. Signature base. For each example request with Signature-Input, tools compute the RFC 9421 signature base from the request; the viewer shows it with each covered component distinguished.
  15. Deferred timeline. When steps return 202 Accepted with a Location, the walkthrough derives the pending request's timeline (each poll and its status) and the viewer shows it.
  16. Artifacts. Scenarios and steps MAY carry artifacts: named JSON or Markdown documents (such as a mission document), optionally with a computed digest (sha-256, base64url) the viewer shows.
  17. Value tracing. The viewer lets the reader select a value (a digest, identifier or thumbprint) and highlights every step, header, body field, token claim and artifact where it appears.
  18. Comparisons. A document MAY declare comparisons: tables whose columns are scenarios and whose rows are questions with a short answer per scenario. The viewer shows them as pages in the navigation.
  19. Pages. A document MAY declare pages: Markdown reference documents placed in a group. The viewer also generates an overview page from the protocol description, roles and groups. Scenarios MAY carry references (name and URL) shown as spec links.
  20. Viewer conveniences: copy buttons on headers, bodies and tokens; a collapsible and resizable details panel, remembered per browser.
  21. Guided tours. A flow MAY carry a tour: ordered beats, each with a focus region and narration (and optional hold milliseconds). Regions name parts of the page generically (diagram, narrative, request.line, request.headers.<name>, request.body[/<json-pointer>], the same for response, token.<id>.header, token.<id>.claims.<claim>, artifact.<id>[/<json-pointer>], lifecycle, page.<id>#<heading>). Validation checks each region resolves against the step.
  22. Focus hook. The viewer exposes window.pidl.focus(scenarioId, step, region), which switches to the tab holding the region, scrolls its panel so the region is visible, highlights it, and resolves after rendering. Autoplay plays a step's beats in order.
  23. Tour drafting. pidl tour draft proposes beats for a step from its example (headers, body fields, token claims) with narration drafted from the glossary, for an author to edit.
  24. Narration per representation. A flow MAY carry representations, keyed by representation (http, curl, or a sample language such as go, typescript, python, csharp), each with its own narration and tour. When the reader picks that representation the viewer and video use them, falling back to the flow's own. Tour regions for these name lines or marked regions of the code (curl.line.<n>, sample.<language>.line.<n>, sample.<language>#<region>).

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• All additions are optional; v0.8.0 documents validate and render unchanged.
  • Check profiles are data plus small Go functions in the analyze package; adding one does not change the core.
  • The viewer remains a single self-contained HTML file.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The AAuth example declares groups and at least one variant, and every step has an ID and narration.
  • The viewer navigates AAuth by section, autoplays a scenario, and shows HTTP, cURL and Go for steps with samples.
  • The example checks report no findings on the AAuth example, and report the digest and algorithm problems when run on a deliberately broken copy.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Variants are scenarios linked by variant_of, so ordering, validation and projection rules apply unchanged.
  • Samples come from tested source files by reference, with inline code allowed for snippets that have no home. Resolved code is embedded at generation time.
  • cURL is generated, never stored.
  • Protocol rules live in profiles, keeping PIDL's core neutral.
  • Ships as v0.9.0.

docs.title: ROADMAP — PIDL for developer content

docs.title: TRD — PIDL for developer content
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-003 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: 1. Types
docs.text:
type Group struct {
    ID          string `json:"id"`
    Name        string `json:"name"`
    Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`
}
// Protocol gains: Groups []Group; Pronunciations map[string]map[string]string
// (term -> language -> spoken form), matching videoascode's pronunciations,
// e.g. {"agent_jkt": {"en-US": "agent J K T"}}. A map is right here: entries
// are looked up by term, never listed in order.
// ProtocolMeta gains: Language string (BCP 47, default "en-US"), the source
// language and fallback for narration.

// Narration is spoken text keyed by BCP 47 language. Always an object, never a
// bare string, so the schema has no union type.
type Narration map[string]string

// Scenario gains: Group, VariantOf, VariantLabel, Narration Narration; Briefing *Briefing
type Briefing struct {
    Why       string    `json:"why,omitempty"`       // why the scenario exists, as prose
    Points    []string  `json:"points,omitempty"`    // key points, in display order
    Narration Narration `json:"narration,omitempty"` // spoken over the briefing slides
}
// Flow gains: ID, Narration Narration, Representations map[string]RepresentationNarration
type RepresentationNarration struct { // keyed by "http", "curl", or a sample language
    Narration Narration  `json:"narration,omitempty"`
    Tour      []TourBeat `json:"tour,omitempty"`
}
// FlowExample and Scenario gain: Samples []Sample
type Sample struct {
    Language string        `json:"language"`         // curl is generated, not stored
    Label    string        `json:"label,omitempty"`
    Role     string        `json:"role,omitempty"`   // entity ID whose developer writes this
    Code     string        `json:"code,omitempty"`
    Source   *SampleSource `json:"source,omitempty"`
}
type SampleSource struct {
    Repo   string `json:"repo"`             // e.g. github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go
    Ref    string `json:"ref,omitempty"`    // tag or commit
    Path   string `json:"path"`
    Region string `json:"region"`
    SHA256 string `json:"sha256,omitempty"` // recorded by resolve
}

Language identifiers follow common highlighter names: go, typescript, javascript, python, csharp, java, curl.

docs.title: 2. Validation
docs.text:
• Group IDs unique; a scenario's group exists.
  • variant_of names a scenario that is not itself a variant, in the same group; variant_label required with it.
  • Flow IDs unique within a scenario; include steps may have IDs.
  • Samples: exactly one of code or source; role names an entity.

docs.title: 3. Sample resolution (samples.go, cmd/pidl samples)
docs.text:
• pidl samples resolve --root <dir> maps repo to a local checkout under <dir> (default $GOPATH/src), extracts the region between pidl:begin <name> and pidl:end <name> (comment syntax per language), dedents it, and records sha256.
  • pidl samples check fails when a region is missing or its hash changed without re-resolving.
  • Generation (walkthrough-json, viewer) embeds resolved code; it never reaches the network.

docs.title: 4. cURL generation (render/curl.go)
docs.text: From ExampleRequest: method, URL, each header as -H, and the body as --data-raw with the exact bytes the digest covers. A comment states that the signature headers are replayed from the example.

docs.title: 5. Example checks (analyze/examples.go)
docs.text:
Generic rules, scope document:

Rule Check EX001 Content-Digest sha-256 equals the digest of the compact JSON body (and of the pretty-printed form, to allow either) EX002 A full compact JWT in a header or body decodes to a decoded token on the same example EX003 Every component in Signature-Input is present as a header or derived component EX004 created is within each presented token's iat..exp EX005 Decoded tokens have exp > iat

Profiles (analyze/profiles): aauth-draft-11 adds AA101 (alg must be fully specified; EdDSA rejected), AA102 (no alg parameter in Signature-Input), AA103 (cnf.jwk carries alg), AA104 (token lifetimes within the draft's limits), AA105 (resource token agent_jkt equals the thumbprint of the presenting key).

protocol.profiles selects profiles; pidl analyze --profile overrides.

docs.title: 6. Walkthrough model
docs.text: Walkthrough gains Groups, Pronunciations; scenarios gain Group, VariantOf, VariantLabel, Narration, Briefing; steps gain ID, Narration, Samples (resolved), Curl, and TokenEvents (issued, forwarded, presented, checked) derived from issues, verifies and example tokens.

docs.title: 7. Viewer
docs.text:
• Left navigation: groups as sections; variants collapse under their base with a toggle in the scenario header.
  • Autoplay: play, pause, replay; speed 0.5×–3×; a step's duration is max(2.5 s, words / 2.7 s⁻¹) from narration, or audio length when video timing is supplied.
  • Token lifecycle panel: per token, the steps where it is issued, forwarded, presented and checked; the active step is highlighted.
  • Representation tabs: HTTP, cURL and one tab per sample language present; the chosen language is remembered per browser.
  • Decoded/raw toggle on tokens.

docs.title: 8. Explorer parity
docs.text:
type GlossaryEntry struct {
    Term        string `json:"term"`                // e.g. "Signature-Key", "agent_jkt"
    Kind        string `json:"kind"`                // header | claim | term
    Category    string `json:"category,omitempty"`  // e.g. "protocol" to badge protocol-defined headers
    Description string `json:"description"`
    Reference   string `json:"reference,omitempty"` // spec section or URL
}
type Artifact struct {
    ID, Name  string
    MediaType string          // application/json | text/markdown
    Content   json.RawMessage // JSON value, or a JSON string for Markdown
    Digest    *ArtifactDigest // {alg: "sha-256", encoding: "base64url", of: "raw"|"canonical-json"}
}
type Comparison struct {
    ID, Name, Group string
    Scenarios []string        // column order
    Rows      []ComparisonRow // {question, answers: map[scenarioID]string}
}
type Page struct {
    ID, Name, Group string
    Markdown        string
}
// Scenario gains References []Reference; Protocol gains Glossary, Comparisons, Pages; scenarios and flows gain Artifacts.
  • Signature base (httpsig.go): build the RFC 9421 base from Signature-Input components: derived components from the URL and method, header fields by name, and @signature-params from the input's parameters. Unknown components are reported as an example check finding.
  • Deferred timeline: derived in the walkthrough from steps whose response is 202 with Location, pairing later polls of that URL until a non-202 response.
  • Value tracing: the walkthrough indexes string values of at least 16 characters across headers, bodies, token claims and artifacts; the viewer highlights matches on selection.
  • Pages render Markdown with a small, dependency-free renderer in the viewer (headings, lists, code, tables, links).

docs.title: 9. Guided tours
docs.text:
type TourBeat struct {
    Focus     string `json:"focus"`
    Narration Narration `json:"narration,omitempty"`
    Hold      int       `json:"hold,omitempty"` // minimum milliseconds on screen
}
// Flow gains Tour []TourBeat
  • Regions resolve against the walkthrough step: header names case-insensitively, JSON pointers per RFC 6901 into bodies, token claims by token definition ID and claim name, artifacts by ID.
  • Viewer elements carry data-pidl-region attributes. window.pidl.focus selects the HTTP or Tokens tab as needed, expands collapsed values, scrolls the panel with behavior: "instant" in video mode, applies a highlight ring, and resolves after two animation frames.
  • Representation regions: curl.line.<n>, sample.<language>.line.<n> and sample.<language>#<region> (a pidl:begin/pidl:end region) resolve against the generated cURL and resolved samples.
  • Validation reports narration that has no text in the source language, and a representation key that is not http, curl or a sample language present on the flow.
  • pidl tour draft emits beats for the step's notable regions (signature headers, challenge headers, body fields, claims the receiver checks) with narration drafted from glossary descriptions; values are not read aloud.

docs.title: Sequencing
docs.text: Types and validation precede sample resolution and checks; walkthrough changes precede viewer work; the AAuth example gains groups, IDs and narration in INIT-PIDL-004, with a small fixture here for tests.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Region markers in SDK repos require SDK maintainers' cooperation. Mitigation: markers are comments, and inline code remains possible.
  • cURL cannot sign. Mitigation: label replayed signatures clearly.
  • Profile rules encode a draft that changes. Mitigation: profiles are versioned by draft (aauth-draft-11).

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Table tests for validation, region extraction (per comment syntax), cURL generation and each check rule; golden walkthrough JSON; viewer unit tests for navigation grouping, autoplay timing and lifecycle derivation.

docs.title: PLAN — Complete AAuth coverage
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-004 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text: INIT-PIDL-003 phases 1–3 delivered (groups, variants, IDs, narration, samples, example checks).

docs.title: Build Order
docs.text:
1. Foundation: example generator in the repository, file split by section, groups, narration and pronunciations for existing scenarios.
  2. Signing and bootstrap.
  3. Interaction, delegation and lifecycle: deferred delivery, step-up, clarification, interaction chaining, call chaining, sub-agents, revocation.
  4. Missions.
  5. R3 and samples: Rich Resource Requests, Go samples, coverage table, release.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Large content volume One section per phase; each phase ships on its own Draft revisions mid-way Generator holds wire details; regenerate on a new draft

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text: Samples in other languages as SDKs are chosen; narrated videos per section (INIT-PIDL-005).

docs.title: PRD — Complete AAuth coverage
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-004 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The AAuth example covers the five resource access modes and three shared steps. AAuth is larger: how agents sign, how they bootstrap on each platform, missions and their governance endpoints, call and interaction chaining, sub-agents, clarification, deferred delivery, step-up, revocation, and the experimental Rich Resource Requests. An existing AAuth explorer shows these areas, but its examples predate draft-11 (non-matching digests, forbidden algorithms) and its code is AAuth-specific. PIDL is to be the source of truth for AAuth walkthroughs, so it needs the whole protocol.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Every area of AAuth draft-11 and its companion drafts, as PIDL scenarios in ordered sections, with variants where a scenario has distinct forms.
  • Each scenario has an introduction and spoken narration; each step has a narrative, narration and, where it is an HTTP exchange, an example.
  • All examples come from the drafts (draft) or their normative text (derived), share one set of keys, identifiers and timeline, and pass the generic checks and the aauth-draft-11 profile.
  • Agent, resource and server roles show Go code from aauth-go's tested examples.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Copying content from other AAuth tools. The explorer is used only as a checklist of topics.
  • Languages other than Go until their SDKs are chosen.
  • Video production (INIT-PIDL-005).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Section Scenarios Source Signing Pseudonymous signing (hwk); agent tokens (jwt); hardware-backed delegation (jkt-jwt); server signing (jwks_uri); comparison draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-09; draft-11 §11.3 Agent bootstrap Web app; iOS; Android; self-hosted; many agents under one operator; web and mobile renewal; sub-agent issuance draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap-02 Resource access Agent identity; resource-managed; person identity; PS authorization; federated authorization; comparison draft-11 §4.2, §6, §7, §9 Interaction and delivery Deferred delivery (202) and polling; step-up; clarification chat; interaction chaining draft-11 §6.5.1, §7.5, §10.1.2, §11.8 Missions Proposal and approval; mission context at a resource; update and completion; permission endpoint; audit endpoint; out-of-bounds access; end-to-end; with and without missions draft-11 §7.7, §7.8, §8 Delegation Call chaining; sub-agents (parent-mediated authorization) draft-11 §10 Lifecycle Revocation draft-11 §11.12 Rich Resource Requests (experimental) Vocabulary-based access; per-call operations; content addressing and consent draft-hardt-aauth-r3

Variants: autonomous and with-user-approval for the PS and federated modes; platform variants under bootstrap.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Scenarios are grouped as in the scope table, in that order.
  2. Shared steps (agent token, person token, consent, deferred polling) are fragments reused across scenarios.
  3. Every HTTP step has an example; the example checks and aauth-draft-11 profile report nothing.
  4. Every scenario and step has narration, and the protocol declares pronunciations for its identifiers.
  5. Agent, resource, PS and AS roles show Go samples from aauth-go for the scenarios it covers, referenced by region.
  6. Findings the analyzer reports against the drafts (such as SEC019 in federated access) remain visible as callouts.
  7. A coverage table in the documentation lists each scenario, its source sections and its status.
  8. Explorer-parity content: an AAuth glossary (every AAuth header, every token claim, key terms); mission documents and R3 documents as artifacts with their digests; comparison tables for signing modes, access modes, and with and without missions; reference pages for the HTTP Signatures profile, the Signature-Key schemes and the error model; and the overview's layers prose.
  9. Tours for the steps that teach the most: signed requests, challenges, resource tokens, the PS-to-AS federation request, mission approval and R3 per-call consent.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The viewer navigates every section in the scope table.
  • pidl analyze --profile aauth-draft-11 reports no example findings.
  • Each Go sample resolves from aauth-go and its region hash is recorded.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Content is written from the drafts. Other tools inform the topic list only.
  • One example world. agent.example, ps.example, resource.example, as.resource.example, the RFC 8037 agent key and one timeline across every scenario, so values link up across the whole protocol.
  • Experimental drafts are labeled in the section name and scenario introductions.

docs.title: TRD — Complete AAuth coverage
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-004 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: 1. File layout
docs.text: examples/aauth_protocol.json grows large. It is split into a base file (protocol, entities, tokens, pronunciations, groups, shared fragments) and one file per section that imports the base's scenarios as needed, composed by extends/imports into the built-in example. Composition already preserves scenario order and fragments.

docs.title: 2. Example generation
docs.text:
The generator used for the current examples moves into the repository as tools/aauthgen (Go), so examples are reproducible:

  • One table of shared values (hosts, keys, identifiers, timeline).
  • Builders for each message type (signed request, 401/202 challenges, token responses, mission documents) that compute real Content-Digest values and encode tokens from their decoded form.
  • Signatures remain placeholders; tokens appear shortened (header.eyJ…) wherever a full compact form would trip secret scanners.
  • go generate ./examples regenerates examples; a test fails when the committed file differs.

docs.title: 3. Sources
docs.text: Each scenario cites draft sections in its introduction; each example cites its source in source. Mission documents follow draft-11 §8.2 blob members; R3 documents follow the R3 draft's vocabulary format.

docs.title: 4. Go samples
docs.text: Samples reference regions in aauth-go's examples/walkthrough tests (INIT-AAUTHGO-001), named <scenario>.<step> (for example federated.ps-to-as). Each step uses the SDK's lower-level calls, so a sample shows one protocol message rather than the whole Transport round trip. samples resolve records hashes; CI runs samples check against aauth-go v0.3.0.

docs.title: 5. Examples checked against real traffic
docs.text: aauth-go's end-to-end tests export a JSON trace (role-named hosts, ordered headers, bodies, and pointers to per-run values). An example check compares each AAuth example with the matching exchange: method, path, status, header names and order, body members and token claim names. Per-run values (signatures, keys, timestamps, nonces) are not compared.

docs.title: Sequencing
docs.text: Requires INIT-PIDL-003 phases 1–3 (groups, variants, IDs, narration, samples, checks). The generator move comes first so every new scenario is produced the same way.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Draft churn. A new draft revision changes wire details. Mitigation: values live in the generator; the profile is versioned by draft.
  • R3 maturity. The R3 draft is experimental. Mitigation: label it and keep it in its own section and file.
  • SDK coordination. Region markers need a change in aauth-go. Mitigation: inline samples as an interim.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Examples regenerate identically; the analyzer and aauth-draft-11 profile report no example findings; every sample resolves; the viewer renders each section (smoke test over the walkthrough JSON).

docs.text:
1. Viewer video mode and window.pidl.goTo.
  2. Per-scenario videoascode configurations with evaluate steps, plus the combined configuration.
  3. Briefing decks with network diagrams.
  4. Compatibility test, guide and release, with an end-to-end AAuth render.
  5. Narration audio: narration export, then viewer playback against a fixture manifest, then packaging once videoascode writes manifests, then multi-language and per-representation video configurations.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation videoascode configuration changes Compatibility test against its types Frames captured before render goTo resolves after render; evaluate awaits it Narration or briefing gaps Fall back to descriptions; INIT-PIDL-004 adds content

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text: Chapter markers from segment timings; captions highlighted from word timings; outro slides with links.

docs.title: PRD — Narrated protocol videos
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-005 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A PIDL walkthrough explains a protocol step by step in a browser. Developer relations also needs videos (MP4 for YouTube and course platforms) where a narrator introduces each scenario and then walks through it while the diagram advances. Producing them by hand means recording the screen, writing and recording narration, building intro slides, and re-editing whenever the protocol or narration changes.

videoascode (vac) already turns a configuration of Marp slides and browser steps with voiceover text into a narrated video: text-to-speech through OmniVoice (ElevenLabs, Deepgram, local F5-TTS), timing each step to its audio, recording, subtitles, audio caching and multiple languages. What is missing is the bridge from PIDL: generated configurations and briefing slides, and a viewer that can be driven to an exact step and captured cleanly.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• One video per scenario, so a scenario re-renders on its own when its content changes, maps to one lecture or playlist entry, and composes into longer videos.
  • Each scenario video opens with briefing slides (title, why the scenario exists, key points, network diagram) and then walks the sequence diagram step by step.
  • PIDL generates everything videoascode needs: a configuration per scenario, a Marp deck per scenario, the viewer page and diagram images.
  • Every captured frame shows the intended step: the viewer exposes a navigation hook that resolves only after the step has rendered.
  • The web viewer speaks too. The narration audio videoascode synthesizes for videos is played in the viewer, in the reader's language and for the representation they chose (HTTP, cURL, Go, TypeScript, Python, C# and others), so the website and the videos sound the same and each clip is paid for once.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Text-to-speech, recording, encoding or subtitles in PIDL. videoascode owns all media work; PIDL only plays the clips it is given.
  • Uploading to YouTube.
  • Writing narration and briefings. They are content (INIT-PIDL-004 for AAuth).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Viewer video mode (?mode=video): presentation stage on, pointer hidden, instant scrolling, hover states off, menu bar reduced to the protocol and scenario name.
  2. Navigation hook: in video mode the viewer exposes window.pidl.goTo(scenarioId, step), which navigates and returns a promise that resolves after the step has rendered and the diagram has scrolled into place. Targets are absolute, so a retried step cannot drift.
  3. generate -f vac writes one videoascode configuration per selected scenario (<NN>-<scenario-id>.vac.yaml), each with:
  4. a slide segment for that scenario's briefing deck;
  5. a browser segment that opens the viewer at the scenario's overview, holds on it with the scenario narration, then runs one evaluate step per walkthrough step calling window.pidl.goTo with that step's narration as its voiceover, and holds briefly at the end.
  6. Tours in video. When a step has a tour, each beat follows the step as its own evaluate step calling window.pidl.focus with the beat's narration as voiceover, so the panel scrolls to and highlights what the narrator is describing, held for exactly that narration. A long panel is covered by several beats.
  7. Combined configuration (--combined): one configuration listing the selected scenarios' segments in navigation order, for a single longer video.
  8. Briefing deck (generate -f marp-briefing): a Marp deck per scenario with speaker notes as voiceover:
  9. title slide: group and scenario name;
  10. why slide: the briefing's why prose;
  11. key points slide: the briefing's points;
  12. network slide: the scenario's roles and trust boundaries as an image rendered by PIDL (svg-network for the scenario projection). Slides without briefing content are omitted; narration falls back to the scenario description.
  13. Selection: --scenario, --group, or all main scenarios; fragments only when asked; navigation order throughout.
  14. Viewer location: a file URL to a generated viewer HTML (default) or an HTTP URL supplied with --viewer-url.
  15. Pronunciations and language: PIDL's pronunciations and protocol.language are written into each configuration unchanged.
  16. Voice settings (--voice-provider, --voice-id, --model) become the configuration's default voice; credentials stay in the environment, where videoascode reads them.

  17. Output layout: one directory per run with the viewer HTML, per-scenario decks, diagram images and configurations, ready for vac browser video --config.

  18. Narration export (generate -f narration): a videoascode narration set with one unit per spoken item: scenario narration (<scenario>), briefing narration (<scenario>/briefing), step narration (<scenario>/<flow-id>) and tour beats (<scenario>/<flow-id>/beat-<n>), each with its texts by language. Representation-specific narration becomes extra units with that representation as the variant. --lang and --representation limit the set.

  19. Viewer audio. When the viewer has an audio manifest, the controls show a speaker button (speaker icon when on, muted speaker when off; off by default and remembered per browser):
    • turning it on plays the current step's clip;
    • forward, back, a click on a step or a deep link stop the current clip and play the new step's clip, then its tour beats' clips in order, focusing each region as its clip starts;
    • play advances when the step's clips finish instead of on the estimated duration, and the speed control sets the playback rate;
    • the language selector and the representation tabs switch the on-screen narration and the audio together;
    • a missing clip, or one whose text hash no longer matches the narration, is skipped silently with timed advance, and the step shows that audio is unavailable.
  20. Audio packaging (generate -f viewer --audio <manifest>): the manifest is embedded in the viewer HTML and the clips copied beside it (audio/clips/…), referenced by relative path, so the page works from a static host or opened as a local file.
  21. Videos per language and representation: generate -f vac --lang en-US,fr-FR,zh-Hans writes each configuration with segment transcripts per language (videoascode's multi-language form, producing one MP4 per language), and --representation curl selects that representation's narration, tours and tab, naming files <NN>-<scenario-id>.<representation>.vac.yaml. Voiceovers carry the same unit IDs as the narration set, so videos and the viewer share clips.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• vac browser video renders an AAuth scenario from its generated configuration into an MP4 that opens with the briefing slides and then shows each step in sync with its narration, with no frame showing the wrong step.
  • Re-running generation after editing one scenario's narration changes only that scenario's files.
  • A combined configuration renders several scenarios into one video.
  • With audio on, pressing play on an AAuth scenario in the viewer narrates every step and beat in French when French is selected, and the cURL narration when the cURL tab is selected, using clips videoascode generated once for both the viewer and the videos.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• videoascode is the media engine; PIDL generates its inputs.
  • One video per scenario is the unit; longer videos are compositions.
  • evaluate with an absolute navigation hook, not key presses: videoascode screenshots right after an action, so the action must not return until the step has rendered.
  • Audio round trip. PIDL supplies the text (narration sets and video configurations); videoascode returns clips and a manifest; PIDL's viewer plays them. Neither tool needs the other's internals: the contract is the narration set and the audio manifest (INIT-VAC-001).
  • No browser speech synthesis fallback by default: voices differ across browsers and would not match the videos.
  • Briefings are content in PIDL (INIT-PIDL-003), so slides, viewer and video share one source.

docs.title: TRD — Narrated protocol videos
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-005 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: How videoascode Runs a Browser Segment
docs.text: From its recorder (pkg/browser/recorder.go): it loads the segment URL, then for each step runs the action, takes one screenshot, and holds that frame for the step's MinDuration, which it sets from the voiceover's audio length plus 500 ms (pkg/segment/browser_segment.go). The evaluate action calls page.Eval, which awaits a returned promise. Slide segments render Marp decks with speaker notes as voiceover. Mixed configurations combine slide and browser segments.

docs.title: 1. Viewer video mode and navigation hook
docs.text:
// Present only with ?mode=video
window.pidl = {
  goTo(scenarioId: string, step: number): Promise<void>,
};

goTo sets the position, waits for React to commit, scrolls the active row into view with behavior: "instant", then waits two animation frames before resolving. Video mode also sets cursor: none, disables transitions and hover styles, and forces the presentation stage.

docs.title: 2. Configuration per scenario (render/vac.go)
docs.text:
version: "1.0"
title: "AAuth: Federated authorization (four-party)"
defaultLanguage: en-US
defaultVoice: { provider: elevenlabs, voiceId: "<--voice-id>" }
resolution: { width: 1920, height: 1080 }
frameRate: 30
pronunciations:
  AAuth: { en-US: "ay auth" }
segments:
  - type: slide
    name: federated-authorization-briefing
    source: decks/05-federated-authorization.md
  - type: browser
    name: federated-authorization
    url: "file:///…/viewer.html?mode=video#federated-authorization/0"
    steps:
      - action: evaluate
        script: "() => window.pidl.goTo('federated-authorization', 0)"
        voiceover: "<scenario narration>"
      - action: evaluate
        script: "() => window.pidl.goTo('federated-authorization', 1)"
        voiceover: "<step 1 narration>"
      # a step with a tour adds one evaluate per beat:
      - action: evaluate
        script: "() => window.pidl.focus('federated-authorization', 12, 'token.resource_token.claims.agent_jkt')"
        voiceover: "<beat narration>"
      # … one step per walkthrough step, then its beats
      - action: wait
        duration: 1500

Beats come from INIT-PIDL-003 tours; region strings are validated against the step and escaped for the script string. Scenario IDs are validated to ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$, so they are safe to embed in the script string. Narration falls back to the step description; a step with neither gets minDuration 2500.

docs.title: 3. Briefing deck (render/marp.go)
docs.text: A Marp deck per scenario with marp: true, a 16:9 size, and one slide per briefing part; each slide's spoken text is an HTML comment, the voiceover format videoascode reads. The network slide embeds images/<NN>-<scenario-id>-network.svg, rendered with the SVG network renderer from the scenario's projection.

docs.title: 4. CLI and output
docs.text:
pidl generate -f vac [--scenario id | --group id | --all] [--combined] [--viewer-url url] [--voice-provider p --voice-id v --model m] -o <dir> <file> writes:

<dir>/
  viewer.html
  decks/<NN>-<scenario-id>.md
  images/<NN>-<scenario-id>-network.svg
  <NN>-<scenario-id>.vac.yaml
  all.vac.yaml            # with --combined

Files are written only when their content changes, so unchanged scenarios keep their videoascode audio caches warm.

docs.title: 5. Narration audio in the viewer
docs.text:
• Export (render/narration.go): walks every selected scenario's walkthrough and emits videoascode's narration set (version, defaultLanguage from protocol.language, pronunciations, units). Unit IDs use flow IDs, never positions, so reordering steps keeps clips.
  • Manifest lookup: the viewer indexes clips by (id, variant, language), falling back from the selected representation to no variant and from the selected language to protocol.language. It computes SHA-256 of the narration text with crypto.subtle and compares it with textSha256; a mismatch is treated as missing.
  • Playback (hooks/useNarrationAudio.ts): one HTMLAudioElement; each navigation increments a token so a late ended event from an earlier clip cannot advance the walkthrough; playbackRate follows the speed control with preservesPitch. The first press of the speaker or play button is the user gesture browsers require before audio can play.
  • Video mode never plays audio; videoascode records audio separately.
  • Packaging: generate -f viewer --audio audio/audio-manifest.json -o site/ embeds the manifest as JSON in the page and copies referenced clips to site/audio/clips/.
  • Multi-language video configurations: steps keep voiceover in the source language; the segment's transcripts carry one segment per voiced step and beat for each language, in step order, as videoascode expects.

The round trip:

pidl generate -f narration -o narration.json aauth.json
vac narration tts --input narration.json --output site/audio --lang en-US,fr-FR,zh-Hans
pidl generate -f viewer --audio site/audio/audio-manifest.json -o site aauth.json
pidl generate -f vac --lang en-US,fr-FR,zh-Hans -o video aauth.json   # videos reuse the cached clips

docs.title: Sequencing
docs.text: Requires INIT-PIDL-003 narration, briefings and pronunciations. Viewer audio requires videoascode's narration export and audio manifest (INIT-VAC-001); the viewer is built against a fixture manifest until then. Video mode and the navigation hook come first, then configurations, then decks.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Configuration drift between PIDL's output and videoascode. Mitigation: a test that parses generated YAML with videoascode's configuration types, pinned by version.
  • Marp rendering differences for SVG images. Mitigation: render network diagrams to PNG as well and prefer PNG in decks if SVG fails.
  • File URLs may be restricted in some setups. Mitigation: --viewer-url.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Golden configuration and deck for the AAuth fixture; viewer unit tests for the navigation hook (resolves after render) and video-mode flags; a test that unchanged scenarios are not rewritten; a documented end-to-end render of one AAuth scenario.

docs.title: PLAN — Postman collections from PIDL
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-PIDL-006

  1. Collection structure: folders, requests, base URL variables and documentation; mock mode can ship with this phase since it needs no signer.
  2. Chaining and checks: captured variables, response checks and polling.
  3. Signer and environments: the aauth-sandbox signer profile and environment files, once the sandbox's signing helper exists (RMI-AAUTHGO-025).
  4. AAuth collection: generated into aauth-dev/aauth-postman with Newman CI against the sandbox image (RMI-AAUTHGO-027).

docs.title: PRD — Postman collections from PIDL
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-006 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A PIDL walkthrough shows a protocol's messages; developers also want to send them. Postman is where many API developers try and test HTTP flows, and a collection that walks a protocol's scenarios step by step, with values passed from one response to the next request, turns the walkthrough into something runnable. Writing such a collection by hand repeats everything the PIDL file already says (order, URLs, headers, bodies, tokens) and drifts as the protocol changes.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• pidl generate -f postman writes a Postman collection (format v2.1) from a PIDL file: one folder per scenario, in output order, with one request per step the client role sends.
  • Requests chain: values a response delivers (tokens, Location URLs) are captured into variables the later requests use.
  • Each request checks its response against the example: status, required headers, body members, and the claims of tokens it carries.
  • Signed protocols run through a signing helper, such as the AAuth sandbox's (INIT-AAUTHGO-002), so Postman needs no cryptography.
  • A mock mode turns example responses into saved Postman examples for a Postman mock server, for exploring without running anything.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Signing inside Postman scripts.
  • Playing server roles in Postman. Server-to-server steps are described in folder documentation, not sent.
  • Publishing to Postman workspaces from PIDL. Publication belongs to the repository that holds a protocol's collection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Structure. A collection per PIDL file with the protocol's name and description; a folder per group, then per scenario, in output order; fragments expanded in place. Folder descriptions carry the scenario description and narration, and list the steps between other roles that the collection does not send.
  2. Client role. --client <role> (default: the first entity of type agent or client) selects the role whose requests become Postman requests.
  3. Requests. Method, URL, headers and body from each step's example request, with each role's base URL replaced by a variable ({{ps_url}}). Signature headers are left out when a signer is configured; they are added by the signer.
  4. Chaining. For tokens a step issues (security.issues) and values in example responses that later requests reuse (matched by value: tokens, Location, pending URLs, codes), the response's test script stores them in collection variables, and later requests refer to the variables.
  5. Checks. Test scripts assert the status code; that headers named in the example are present; that body members in the example are present; and, for tokens in the example, that the token decodes and carries the example's claim names. Values that change per run are not compared.
  6. Deferred responses. A 202 with Location is followed by a polling request that repeats until the final status or a retry limit, using Postman's request flow controls.
  7. Signer. --signer <url> sends requests through a signing helper by prefixing the target URL; the token a step presents (from the example's Signature-Key token) is passed in the helper's presentation headers, named by --signer-profile aauth-sandbox.
  8. Person steps. Steps where a person acts in a browser are described, not sent; --approve-url adds a request to a headless approval endpoint for automated runs.
  9. Mock mode. --mock saves each step's example response as a Postman example on its request and points base URLs at {{mock_url}}; no signer, no checks beyond status.
  10. Environments. generate -f postman-environment writes environment files for named targets from a small targets file (role base URLs, signer URL), for example sandbox, Docker, minikube and mock.
  11. Validation. The generated collection validates against Postman's published v2.1 collection schema.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The AAuth collection runs green in Newman against the AAuth sandbox for all five access modes.
  • The mock-mode collection, imported into Postman with a mock server, steps through every scenario.
  • Changing an example in the PIDL file changes only the affected requests in the generated collection.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Generated, never hand-edited. The PIDL file is the source of truth; protocol repositories commit the generated collection.
  • Signing stays out of Postman. A signing helper is simpler and works the same in Postman, Newman and curl.
  • The AAuth collection lives in aauth-dev/aauth-postman, with its environments, workshop guide and a Newman CI job against the sandbox image.
